read.n_items: Meta-benchmark: 46 best-practice criteria (14 design, 10 implementation, 19 documentation, 3 maintenance per App. J) applied to 24 AI benchmarks (16 foundation-model + 8 non-FM), ~1,104 criterion-level judgments. Criteria derived from a literature review (AI plus bioinformatics, environmental science, transistor hardware, optimization, education testing) and unstructured interviews with 20+ stakeholders across 5 groups, refined in 3 iterative phases; each benchmark scored 0/5/10/15 (or n/a) per criterion by at least two authors independently with mandatory consensus (third-reviewer escalation defined, never needed); only developer-released sources (papers, websites, GitHub) admissible.
read.key_stats: Stage means 0-15 scale (FM/non-FM/All): Design 10.6/11.2/10.8; Implementation 5.5/7.5/6.2 (weakest); Documentation 10.3/9.9/10.1; Maintenance 9.1/10.6/9.6. Overall design mean 10.7 (text; Table 1 says 10.8), weighted usability 8.7. Criterion lows: replication script 3.75/15, statistical significance 5.62/15. 14/24 benchmarks report no significance/uncertainty and no repeated evaluations; 17/24 lack replication scripts (4 more partial); build status 3/24; GUID/canary contamination defenses only in GPQA and BIG-bench. MMLU lowest weighted average 5.5 vs GPQA 11.0. FM vs non-FM difference not significant (bootstrap, 95% CI). Design-usability Pearson: All rho=0.693 p<0.001, FM rho=0.730 p=0.001, non-FM rho=0.477 p=0.279 (n=8). No inter-rater kappa reported (consensus protocol only); no human baseline (n/a, humans are the raters); cost not reported (manual scoring, standard laptops, uncompensated volunteer interviewees).
implications: State determinism and split the noise budget: BetterBench's significance criterion (App. J.3 #17) explicitly requires deterministic benchmarks to say so and others to report variance bounds; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN should document 'label noise ~0 by construction' and report intra-model variance from >=5 repeated runs per model x condition (seeds/temperatures), using the paper's intra-vs-inter variance framing to justify any model-ranking claim.

Size from the 1%-detectability rule with template-level clustering (Sec. 5): at target single-digit pass rates (p~0.05), detecting a 1-point difference needs effective n ~1,900 independent items and a 3-5-point gap needs ~200-500, but instances within a template are correlated, so 8 templates cannot support significance regardless of instance count; scale to ~30-50 independent templates x 20+ instances x >=3 repeats and report template-clustered bootstrap CIs by default.

Adopt the contamination stack almost nobody uses (J.2 #6-7): embed canary GUIDs in every generated artifact, publish only key-protected-encrypted instances (plain obfuscation is auto-decompressed by crawlers, per [36]), hold back a private seed pool to regenerate fresh instances per release, and ship a training_on_test_set probe; add release requirements (App. H pattern) forbidding training on instance text - this directly fixes the leak of method recipes and answer menus that caused the 94-100% saturation.

Report random and human performance per condition (J.1 #10-11): compute the exact random chain-pass floor from the generator (product of per-stage guess rates under non-compensatory scoring - near zero; publish per template), and run a domain-expert human baseline on a stratified subsample including the flawed-premise/refusal condition, or write the explicit n/a justification; without both, single-digit frontier scores cannot be distinguished from a broken benchmark.

Use input-sensitivity variants as both robustness measure and anti-leak fix (J.1 #12): generate k>=3 semantically equivalent paraphrases per instance with no recipe scaffolding and free-response instead of answer menus, report variance across phrasings, and reuse that variance as the intra-model noise estimate for the power analysis.

Validate the stage-level scorer as an 'automatic evaluation' claim (J.1 #13): the deterministic final-answer check is self-validating, but stage credit assignment and refusal detection are judge-like parsing; human-audit sampled transcripts per condition and report scorer-human agreement before the next campaign - a mis-parsed refusal flips the sign of the flawed-premise condition.

Bank the cheap usability points 21/24 benchmarks miss: one-command replication script (field mean 3.75/15), CI build status (3/24 had it), requirements file, quick-start, feedback channel, named contact, license, DOI, Croissant metadata; ship the filled-out App. I.1 checklist inside the release/1.0.0 package to sit above every benchmark BetterBench assessed on implementation.

Version the saturation event instead of patching (Sec. 5, App. B): freeze the saturated 8x~18 release as v1, mark it retired/saturated with a documented post-mortem in Limitations, and release the hardened design as v2 (AgentBench v0.1->v0.2 precedent); silent overwrites destroy comparability and fail the documented-limitations criterion.

Pre-commit score interpretation guidance (J.1 #7): state that chain-pass rate measures multi-stage judgment on synthetic-but-internally-valid science and explicitly disclaim inference to real-lab discovery competence (the construct-validity gap Sec. 8 leaves open), preventing the MMLU/GPQA-style misreporting pattern Sec. 7 documents.
quotes: "benchmarks get an average score of 3.75 on Including a script to replicate results and an average score of 5.62 on Reporting statistical significance." (Sec. 6)
"Yet, 14 out of 24 benchmarks did not perform multiple evaluations of the same model or report statistical significance or uncertainty of results." (Sec. 7)
"For instance, the widely-used MMLU benchmark scored the lowest in our assessment (weighted average: 5.5), while GPQA scored significantly higher (weighted average: 11.0)." (Sec. 7)

read.n_items: N/A - survey paper, constructs no benchmark. Narrative review of 184 references (no systematic search protocol; representative works hand-picked): 4 contamination severity levels (semantic/information/data/label); detection taxonomy = 2 families, 6 method types (7 matching-based + 6 comparison-based works discussed in depth); mitigation taxonomy = 3 families, 6 method types; 7 task areas assessed for BDC vulnerability; 5 future directions. 31 pages: ~19 content + ~12 references; no appendices.
read.key_stats: Survey has no own scores, human baseline, judge, or cost figures; all relayed numbers are point estimates with zero uncertainty reporting (no CIs, clustering, or significance tests anywhere). Relayed headline stats: GPT-3 used 13-gram overlap and GPT-4 a 50-character overlap as decontamination signals; Golchin & Surdeanu guided-instruction detection hit 92-100% accuracy on 7 datasets (contamination found in AG News, WNLI, XSum via GPT-4); Li et al. audit of 15+ LLMs on 6 MCQA benchmarks found 1-45% contamination with larger models benefiting more; paraphrase fine-tuning lets a 13B match GPT-4 on overfit benchmarks and EAL gains up to 15% while evading all tested detectors; EvoEval transformations cut 51 LLMs' HumanEval scores by 39.4% on average; GPT-4 declines sharply on Codeforces problems released after Sep 2021; TreeEval reaches high correlation with AlpacaEval2.0 using ~45 questions; Chatbot Arena had 240K+ votes.
implications: Classify CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's saturation as Information-Level contamination delivered in-context: the survey's level-2 category (metadata, label distributions) exactly covers leaked method recipes and answer menus in prompts. Add a pre-release gate that audits every prompt component against the four levels; anything exposing the recipe (information level) or enumerating answers (in-context label level) gets cut or moved server-side.

Invert TS-Guessing/DCQ detection methods into template QA unit tests: mask the planted defect location, correct stage decision, or refusal trigger, and check whether frontier models guess it above chance from surface features without executing the chain. Any template where masked-slot guessing succeeds is leaking structure; this costs a few hundred calls per template and predicts saturation before a campaign.

String-level novelty buys nothing (13B matches GPT-4 via paraphrase fine-tuning; EAL gains up to 15% undetected): never publish the full instance set or generator parameter space, keep a sealed seed range for official runs, regenerate fresh instances per campaign (dynamic-benchmark strategy), and treat any shipped example instances as burned since rephrase-tuning transfers to same-template siblings.

Answer the scale question at the template/cluster level: deterministic-generator instances within a template are correlated, so effective N for between-model inference is the number of independent templates, not 8x18=144. Use cluster-robust SEs with template as cluster; 8 clusters is far too few - plan on the order of 30-60 independent templates with >=3 repeated decodes per instance to separate decode variance from item variance before claiming significant model differences.

Re-harden the 8 saturated templates with EvoEval/MPA-style targeted transformations (which recovered 39.4% average headroom on 51 LLMs): remove answer menus entirely in favor of free-form exact-match answers (survey notes MCQ formats are more guessable and more contamination-sensitive), compose two templates' chains into one instance, and inject plausible irrelevant context; measure per-transformation pass-rate deltas to identify which leak carried the saturation.

Version and timestamp the generator and keep two instance vintages per campaign (one released earlier, one generated at scoring time): a future model scoring anomalously better on the older vintage reproduces the survey's chronological-analysis contamination signal (Codeforces post-Sep-2021 discontinuity) as a permanent cheap leakage alarm for CRUCIBLE-CHAIN itself.

Adopt private-benchmark hygiene from Jacovi/Chandran for the release package: encrypt any public instance archive with a public key so crawlers ingest ciphertext, never post instances adjacent to answers, embed canary strings in released instances so future ingestion is detectable via membership inference, and keep official scoring behind a harness rather than shipping the answer-computing generator; assume CRUCIBLE-CHAIN 1.0's shipped prompts are in 2026-2027 training corpora.

Keep scoring deterministic and refuse LLM-judge partial credit: the survey repeatedly warns judge LLMs inherit contamination from their own training data. Constructed-truth exact-match non-compensatory scoring is the design that sidesteps this entire surface; for stage-level diagnostics, score stages programmatically against the generator's intermediate values.

Differentiate by reporting what no surveyed work reports: pre-register the inference plan (template clusters, repeats, paired permutation tests across the three conditions), publish CIs on every headline number, and publish leakage-probe and vintage-discontinuity results alongside scores - the survey shows the field reports contamination effects (1-45%, +15%, -39.4%) exclusively as bare point estimates.

read.n_items: 270 tasks = 90 papers (45 train / 45 test) x 3 difficulty levels (Easy: code output given; Medium: Dockerfile+README; Hard: README only), with 181 unique manually-authored task questions (1-8 per paper) shared across levels. Constructed by filtering 5,090 CodeOcean capsules by discipline (CS 37 / social science 28 / medicine 25), language (Python or R), and 10 explicit criteria (README present, <45 min runtime, simple run command, labeled outputs, low output variance, <10 GB, locally reproducible); the 5 authors manually wrote questions about outputs of verified runs and manually reproduced every capsule 3 times to fix ground truth (no external annotators, no inter-rater stats).
read.key_stats: Best agent CORE-Agent+GPT-4o (test set, mean of 3 runs): Easy 60.00% (Table A3: 60.60%+/-4.51%), Medium 57.78%+/-4.51%, Hard 21.48%+/-2.60% (95% CIs from n=3 repeats); GPT-4o-mini 44.44%+/-13.52% / 32.59%+/-11.34% / 16.30%+/-2.60%; unmodified AutoGPT+GPT-4o only 6.67% on Hard (single run, no CI). No human skilled baseline - ground truth is the authors' 3 manual reproductions; scoring is deterministic (no LLM judge): report.json values must fall within a 95% prediction interval from the 3 runs (only 17/181 questions stochastic), and ALL questions per task must be right (non-compensatory). Vision vs written (Easy, GPT-4o): 59.26% vs 87.88%. pass@3 31.1% vs pass-and-3 8.89% on Hard (GPT-4o) - large run-to-run stochasticity. Cost: $4/task cap; successes average $0.54 vs $2.59 for failures; raising cap to $10 moved GPT-4o Hard only 26%->31% (train). Harness: parallel Azure VMs cut evaluation from >20 days sequential to ~2 hours. No significance tests or clustered SEs anywhere.
implications: Scale for significance: CORE-Bench's comparisons rest on only 45 test papers per level plus n=3 full-benchmark repeats, yielding 95% CIs of +/-2.6 to +/-13.5 pp - barely enough to separate 21% from 16%. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's 8 templates x ~18 instances is 144 items but only 8 independent clusters; instances within a template are correlated, so effective n for template-level claims is 8. To defend a single-digit frontier pass-rate claim, grow to on the order of 40-90 independent templates (CORE's paper count), compute standard errors clustered at the template level, and run >=3 repeats per model like CORE's Table A3.

Adopt CORE's guess-proofing rule verbatim: every task has 'at least one question that cannot be solved by guessing (e.g. a question with an open-ended numerical answer)' and all questions must be right. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's leaked answer menus converted open-ended stages into multiple choice; require every chain (ideally every stage) to demand a generator-computed numeric value with no enumerable answer space, and audit prompts for anything that shrinks the answer space to a pickable list.

Difficulty is an information-provisioning dial: the SAME 181 questions score 60% (output handed over), 58% (Dockerfile given), and 21% (README only). CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's 94-100% saturation is diagnostic of accidentally running at the Easy rung - leaked method recipes are CORE's Dockerfile. Strip procedural scaffolding from the headline condition (state goal and data, not pipeline), and keep scaffolded variants only as a diagnostic ladder for localizing failure.

Treat prompt hints as a quantified contaminant: a few days of hint-writing (CORE-Agent's Table 4 prompts plus a report-format check) lifted GPT-4o-mini from 8.9% to 44.4% on Easy and GPT-4o from 6.7% to 21.5% on Hard - a 3-5x swing. Institutionalize a hint audit for CRUCIBLE-CHAIN: any prompt text naming a method, tool, ordering, or answer format is a lever worth tens of points; measure it by running clean vs hinted prompt variants as an explicit ablation.

Report pass@k AND pass-and-k with >=3 repeats: CORE's Hard numbers go 22.2% (pass@1) -> 31.1% (pass@3) but collapse to 8.89% (pass-and-3), showing much of the passing is stochastic. At CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's single-digit target, pass@k vs pass-and-k distinguishes emerging capability from lottery tickets; and the current 94-100% saturation should be re-examined under pass-and-k before concluding the bench is dead.

Exploit the constructed-truth advantage CORE lacks: CORE's contamination defense is a promise ('periodic updates ... could mitigate concerns about contamination and saturation') while its test set and answers sit public on GitHub. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's deterministic generator can mint fresh instances per evaluation: never publish concrete test instances, publish the generator plus a commitment hash, rotate seeds per model release, and keep a sealed template holdout mirroring CORE's 45/45 train/test split (develop prompts only on the dev half).

Define an explicit per-stage tolerance policy: CORE scores within a 95% prediction interval from 3 reference runs and reports exactly which questions are stochastic (17/181). CRUCIBLE-CHAIN should publish a per-stage tolerance spec (exact match / relative epsilon / interval) so near-miss adjudication is not an invisible judge - and note CORE's blind spot that value-only matching credits right-number-from-wrong-figure answers (their own D.3.1 example); scoring all intermediate stages, not just the final value, is the mitigation CRUCIBLE-CHAIN already has - keep it.

Instrument and cap cost; failures are where budget dies: CORE caps at $4/task, finds successes cost $0.54 vs $2.59 for failures (stuck dependency/retry loops), and shows via a $4-vs-$10 ablation that the cap barely binds (26%->31%). At single-digit pass rates ~90%+ of CRUCIBLE-CHAIN spend will be failed runs: set per-chain cost/step caps, log cost per condition (clean/planted-defect/flawed-premise), and run a cap-sensitivity ablation to prove the cap is not producing the low scores.

Design anti-lookup and refusal-neutral scaffolds up front: CORE had to patch its harness mid-flight after an agent web-searched its own CodeOcean capsule and even tried to create an account (D.3.4), and CORE's shipped prompt constraint 'There is no task that you cannot do, so you should not refuse a request by saying you cannot do it' would make CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's flawed-premise condition (where refusal is correct) unpassable. Ensure the harness is network-isolated and that scaffold text neither forbids nor telegraphs refusal.

Keep construction cheaper than solving and document rejections: CORE built on pre-verified CodeOcean capsules and shows its rejection evidence (capsule 826891's spike probability swung 0.423 -> 0.783 across two runs, so it was cut for high variance). CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's generator already satisfies the cost principle; copy the rejection discipline by running each template's reference pipeline multiple times/environments and dropping or interval-izing any stage whose ground truth is environment-sensitive, with an audit trail of rejected instances.

read.n_items: 580 problem-solution pairs claimed (Table 3 itemization sums to 578) across 10 tasks in 6 domains, from 429 published papers: DFT-S/P/C 74 each, MPV 17, HFD 15, HFE 38, QECC 65, GEO 19, BIOGR 138, PDB 64. Constructed by 1-3 PhD-level domain experts per domain from permissively-licensed real papers (S2ORC, arXiv search, EC Zoo, Protein Data Bank); iterative format design, pilot phase, adjudication, then annotator cross-review (agreement >95% HFE/DFT-S, >80% MPV, >90% GEO). Avg input ~15k words, avg ground-truth output 954 words.
read.key_stats: Best average normalized performance 32% (Claude-3 Opus best overall; Gemini 2.0 Flash/Claude most consistent). Per-task single-run results: HFE ROUGE-L up to 50.06 (Gemini 2.0 Flash); HFD max 22.86; GEO max 29.69; QECC max 23.50; DFT R-L 8-14; LLMSim-F1: DFT-S max 35.28, DFT-P max 22.13, MPV max 36.99; BIOGR IoU 0.34-0.49 closed models (0.00 open, no multimodal); PDB identity ratio 0.56 (2.0 Flash) down to 0.00-0.13 (GPT-4o 0.13 due to repetition collapse). Human baseline: NONE - explicitly declared infeasible (no cross-domain expert exists; per-domain experts would double annotation cost). CIs: none; single run per model per task (BIOGR 3 runs); no significance tests; authors concede closed-model differences 'not significant' given 25-75% inter-example spread. Judge agreement: LLMSim precision/recall 'closely match' human experts but validated on only 2 of 9 models; LMScore (GPT-4o log-prob 3-point) correlates with expert good/ok/bad ratings on 10-12% audited samples, no coefficient reported, authors say it 'requires further analysis prior to wider usage'. Cost: not reported. Contamination defenses: none (QECC ground truths are public EC Zoo YAMLs; PDB sequences public; HFD derivations published in Pan et al. 2024).
implications: Recipe leakage is survivable only when execution is the bottleneck: CURIE's HFD hands models the full 13-19 step template yet stays hardest (R-L ~22) because each step demands symbolic derivation, while pattern-matchable extraction (HFE) hits ~50. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN should strip stage enumeration and answer menus from prompts (like DFT-C: state only the goal); if stage structure must stay for scoring, make each stage answer a free computation over instance data that no menu can contain, and verify per-template that a judgment-free recipe-following script still fails the planted-defect condition.

Scale question of record: CURIE's per-task n of 15-74 with one run and no clustering yielded rankings its own authors call not significant. With non-compensatory binary scoring and within-template correlation, CRUCIBLE's 8x18 has effective n closer to 8 than 144. Target >=25-30 independent templates (CURIE's 10 tasks is the floor; its n=15 task is where rankings collapse), 3-5 repeats per item (CURIE found run variance concentrates on hard items, exactly the single-digit-pass regime), template-level bootstrap CIs, and plan several hundred scored chains per model per condition to detect ~5-point model gaps at single-digit pass rates.

Constructed truth eliminates CURIE's entire evaluation stack (two novel LLM judges, leniency prompts, 10-12% human audits, still 'requires further analysis'): protect that advantage by keeping every stage answer in a rigid typed schema scored by a deterministic normalizer, never an LLM matcher, and report unparsable-answer rate separately - CURIE conflated formatting compliance with capability (GPT-4o's HFD score was destroyed by JSON artifacts).

Contamination: CURIE's ground truths are public and memorizable with zero discussion of it; CRUCIBLE's generator-computed labels cannot pre-exist, but the 8x18 instances used in the saturated campaign are now burned. Regenerate fresh instances from held-back seeds each campaign, keep generator parameter distributions private, and add a canary check comparing burned vs fresh sibling instances to flag memorization.

Refusal has an instruction- and temperature-sensitive base rate CURIE measured by accident (models refused despite 'please guess anyway'; lowering temperature increased refusals): score the flawed-premise condition as refusal-with-correct-diagnosis (must name the defect), measure false-refusal rate on clean controls at matched temperature, and report the discrimination margin between conditions rather than bare refusal frequency.

Exhaustive-aggregation is CURIE's durable hardness (find-ALL tasks scored F1 7-37 vs ~50 for single-needle extraction, recall the binding constraint, degrading with item count and dispersion): add CRUCIBLE stages of the form 'identify ALL X in the generated data' whose found set feeds downstream stages, so one miss propagates to chain failure under non-compensatory scoring - completeness cannot be faked from a leaked menu because the item set varies per instance.

Difficulty calibration must be empirical: CURIE's expert easy/medium/hard ratings did not discriminate at the top (medium ~ hard performance, hard examples scarce). Validate CRUCIBLE's difficulty knobs (stage count, wrong-path attractiveness) against measured per-instance pass rates each campaign, retire knobs that do not move the curve, and oversample the empirically-hard tail.

Report per-cell, never composite: CURIE's headline 32% averages incommensurable metrics (ROUGE-L, F1, IoU, identity ratio) over unbalanced tasks and its prose contradicts its tables in at least four places (580 vs 578 items, 75 vs 74 papers, three mutually inconsistent BIOGR IoU ranges, Table 5 vs Table 1 cells). Publish the full condition x template x model pass-rate matrix with exact binomial or bootstrap CIs, keep headlines per-condition, and machine-generate all tables from one results store.

read.n_items: No new benchmark - this is a statistics methodology paper (Evan Miller, Anthropic, 14 pp). It analyzes existing evals: MATH 5,000 questions; HumanEval 164; MGSM 2,500 questions in 250 clusters (same problem x ~10 languages); DROP 9,622 questions / 588 passage-clusters; RACE-H 3,498 / 1,045 clusters; QuAC and SQuAD named as clustered. Framework treats eval questions as iid (or cluster-iid) draws from a hypothetical infinite super-population.
read.key_stats: No model scores, human baselines, or judges - a methods paper. Real-data result (Table 4, Anthropic models): clustered vs naive SE ratios DROP 3.05x (1.34 vs 0.44), MGSM 1.88x, RACE-H 1.10x. Power example: n~969 independent questions to detect a 3-point model difference at alpha=0.05/power 0.8 with omega^2=1/9 - hence 'new evals should contain at least 1,000 questions'. Resampling K=2/4/6 cuts variance by 1/3, 1/2, 5/9 (ceiling 2/3, achieved exactly by next-token probabilities); K 1-to-10 shrinks MDE 13.2% to 7.5% at n=198. Paired differences at corr 0.5 cut variance 1/3. T=0 sampling can triple Var(x) (1/12 to 1/4) and bias means (2/3 to 3/4). Llama 3 CIs shown to be too wide (Bernoulli SE on F1 scores) and too narrow (unclustered reading-comprehension evals).
implications: Templates are clusters: instances from one template share recipe, structure, and the attractive wrong path, so scores correlate within template and effective n collapses toward the number of templates (8), not items (~144). Always report template-clustered SEs (Eq 4) plus both item and cluster counts; the paper's real 3.05x DROP inflation is the mild case since CRUCIBLE has 18 highly-correlated instances per cluster. Power grows with independent template count, not instances per template.

Answer the scale question of record with the paper's power formula n=(z_a/2+z_b)^2(omega^2+sigma_A^2/K_A+sigma_B^2/K_B)/delta^2 (Eq 9) using Appendix C clustered variants, with omega^2 and sigma^2 estimated from the 828-run pilot (divide by K-1). With paired omega^2~0.1, detecting a 10-point frontier-model gap at alpha=.05/power .8 needs ~78 independent templates; 5 points needs ~314; the paper's own 3-point example needs ~969 units. Eight templates cannot support any between-model significance claim - plan tens-to-hundreds of templates and publish the shipped MDE via Eq 10.

Set repeats K by the rule E[sigma_i^2]/K << Var(x): chain tasks cannot use the next-token-probability shortcut (explicitly limited to non-chain-of-thought evals), so resampling is the only conditional-variance lever. Score each instance as mean-of-K, compute SEs across instances clustered by template - never pool K*N runs (inconsistent per Sec 3.1). Once E[sigma^2]/K << Var(x), spend budget on new templates instead of more repeats.

Do not fix noise or saturation by dropping temperature to 0: Sec 3.3 shows T=0 rounds latent pass-probabilities into 0/1, inflating Var(x) up to ~5x and biasing the estimand. Evaluate at deployment temperature with K repeats; also treat the '94-100% saturated' claim itself as an estimate needing clustered SEs - at 8 clusters those CIs are wide.

Use paired clustered differences (Eq 8) for every claim: conditions (clean / planted defect / flawed premise) share generator seeds, so clean-vs-defect drops and refusal deltas are natural within-instance paired differences with free variance reduction (1/3 at corr 0.5, likely more here). Report Table 5 style: difference, paired SE, 95% CI, correlation, clustered at template level; same for before/after leak-fix comparisons.

Non-compensatory all-stages scoring makes instance outcomes exactly Bernoulli, so Eq 2 applies at instance level - but stage-level partial-credit diagnostics are fractional and need SE_CLT (Eq 1), the precise error the paper catches in Llama 3. The 5-8 stages of one chain are one observation; instance is the unit, template is the cluster.

Adopt the reporting standard in the release package: SE in parentheses under every score, n items and n templates in every table, paired CIs instead of bolded maxima, and a stated alpha/power/MDE so consumers can judge what the eval can detect. At single-digit target pass rates supplement normal +/-1.96SE intervals with Wilson/exact binomial CIs (boundary regime the paper ignores), and with <~30 templates use wild-cluster bootstrap or t(G-1) inference since plain sandwich clustered SEs are optimistically small in the few-cluster regime the paper never warns about.

read.n_items: "Hundreds" of problems - exact N never disclosed in the paper. Hand-authored original problems by 60+ expert mathematicians (grad students to faculty, 14 IMO golds collectively, one Fields Medalist contributor; Tao contributed several) under four requirements: originality, automated verifiability (integer or SymPy answers), guessproofness (<1% guess-success rule of thumb), computational tractability (author scripts <1 min). Each problem has a solution, verification script, subject/technique metadata, and 3-dimension difficulty rating; each got at least one blind domain-expert peer review. 35 problems got second review (30 random + 5 released as public samples); coverage spans 70% of top-level MSC2020 subjects (number theory 17.8% of tags, combinatorics 15.8%, group theory 8.9%).
read.key_stats: All six evaluated models (o1-preview, o1-mini, GPT-4o 2024-08-06, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2024-10-22, Grok 2 Beta, Gemini 1.5 Pro 002) scored under 2% mean accuracy (Figure 6: mean over 8 runs; body text inconsistently says single evaluation); no confidence intervals reported anywhere, CIs explicitly deferred to future work. Pass@8: o1-preview ~6%, Grok 2 ~2% (3x inflation over mean for o1-preview). Repeat trials on the 4 ever-solved problems (5 runs/model/problem) swung 0-100%; only one cell (o1-preview, problem 2) was 5/5. One solved problem yielded to simple simulation guessing. Label error: 2/35 double-reviewed problems had wrong answers (Jeffreys posterior 6.9%; authors adopt ~10% critical error rate), plus 6/35 missing hypotheses and 2/35 guessproofness violations. No measured human baseline - difficulty is expert self-report in hours (Background 1-5 / Creativity / Execution) and first-vs-second reviewer ratings "rarely matched." Inter-model harness stats: o1-preview 1.29 responses/problem vs Grok 3.81; Claude/GPT-4o/Grok exceed the 10,000-token limit on >45% of attempts (12k-17k tokens) vs Gemini ~6k (16.8%). Saturation contrast: best-model accuracy 98.1% MMLU-CollegeMath, 96.4% GSM8K, 94.8% MATH, 74% AIME, 60.54% Omni-MATH vs <2% FrontierMath. Cost not reported. Scoring is fully automated binary verification (exact integer / SymPy simplify / custom script) - no LLM judge, no human grading.
implications: Never ship answer menus; enforce a quantitative guessproofness budget: adopt FrontierMath's <1% guess-probability rule per instance - strip enumerable option sets and method recipes from prompts (the exact leak that saturated CRUCIBLE-CHAIN at 94-100%), make the generator emit answers from a space of >=10^4 plausible values, and audit empirically with a no-reasoning forced-immediate-answer baseline that must score <1% per template.

Audit statement error even with near-zero label error: FrontierMath's expert pipeline still had 2/35 wrong answers and 6/35 missing hypotheses despite blind review; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's defect risk migrates from labels to rendered prompts (ambiguity, leaks). Second-review >=30 random rendered instances per release by a non-author, publish a Jeffreys (k+0.5)/(n+1) defect-rate bound, and hold statement-defect rate well below the single-digit target pass rate or it dominates the signal.

Scale answer for the question of record: templates, not instances, are the unit of inference. FrontierMath could not order models or give CIs because successes were rare and correlated ('individual successes can have an outsized impact on rankings'). At target p~0.05, a naive binomial 95% CI of +/-2% needs ~450 independent items, but within-template correlation shrinks effective n toward the template count - 8 templates gives a useless cluster-robust CI (~+/-5-8%). Grow to >=30-50 independent templates x 15-30 instances (500-1000+ runs per condition), bootstrap CIs over templates as clusters, and run >=5 repeats per model x instance since FrontierMath saw 0-100% swings across 5 runs on identical items.

Report mean pass@1 vs pass@k as a headline instability diagnostic: o1-preview went <2% mean to ~6% pass@8. For chains with attractive wrong paths, a large mean-vs-pass@k gap flags templates escapable by resampling luck rather than judgment; publish both plus per-template variance and prune high-gap templates.

Exploit the deterministic generator for contamination defenses FrontierMath could only approximate operationally (encryption, Quetext/Copyscape chosen to avoid training-data retention, admitted plain-email lapse, sponsor access to problems unaddressed despite the OpenAI acknowledgment): keep generator and seeds private, regenerate fresh instance sets per evaluation round, never score on released instances, publish only retired instances plus template descriptions, and document exactly who has seen live instances.

Red-team every template for shortcut circumvention before acceptance: FrontierMath reviewers repeatedly caught brute-force circumvention and one of the four ever-solved problems fell to 'a few simple simulations' - correct answer without correct reasoning. Run an adversarial pass with a frontier model explicitly prompted to find shortcuts/simulation/menu-elimination attacks; accept a template only if attack success stays under the guessproofness budget; re-audit on any prompt change.

Replace subjective difficulty ratings with measured per-stage failure curves: FrontierMath's author-hours ratings 'rarely matched' between reviewers and were validated only informally against GPT-4o solve rates. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN controls difficulty parametrically (chain length, distractor attractiveness, defect subtlety), so calibrate empirically - measure per-stage failure and full-chain pass rates and tune parameters toward single-digit frontier pass rates.

Keep verification fully mechanical but instrument the harness separately: report format-failure rates apart from substantive failures (FrontierMath marked malformatted answers incorrect and three models blew the 10,000-token limit on >45% of attempts - a budget confound), score refusal/flag in the flawed-premise condition as a distinct verified outcome (FrontierMath has no refusal-correct condition; its 6/35 missing-hypothesis problems show malformed statements occur but are treated as noise, so CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's third condition is a defensible novelty), and set token/tool budgets generous enough that budget exhaustion does not masquerade as incapability.

read.n_items: 448 four-option MCQs (main set); 546 extended, 198 diamond, from 564 collected (18 kept as unreleased held-out). Commissioned from 61 Upwork contractors with PhDs (held or in progress) in biology/physics/chemistry subdomains via a 4-stage pipeline: expert writes question + per-option explanations -> same-domain expert validation #1 -> writer revision -> expert validation #2 -> 3 non-expert validations (PhDs in other domains, adjacency exclusions, >=15 min each, web allowed, LLMs banned). Main set drops questions where both experts erred AND all 3 non-experts succeeded; diamond requires 2/2 expert agreement AND <=1/3 non-experts correct (with manual re-admission of questions where the erring expert demonstrably made a mistake, per an 8-category taxonomy of all 191 second-expert misses).
read.key_stats: Human experts: first validator 66.5%+/-4.0%, second 64.8%+/-4.0% (95% CIs, extended set); post-hoc objectivity estimate 73.6-76.4% (abstract: 74%); skilled non-experts 34.1%+/-2.3% despite avg 37 min/question with web access; chance 25%. Subset human numbers (main 71.9/30.4, diamond 81.3/22.1) flagged as selection-skewed. Models (extended/main/diamond): best closed-book Few-shot CoT GPT-4 38.7/39.7/38.8; GPT-4+search with backoff 39.4/41.0/38.8 (raw search only 28.2/28.7/27.6 with 37.2-41.3% abstention); Llama-2-70B-chat and GPT-3.5 at 24.0-31.1 (~chance). GPT-4 CoT by domain: biology 58.1, physics 37.0, chemistry 31.8. Agreement/quality: sufficient-expertise self-report 90.7/93.5/97.0% across sets; of 191 second-expert misses, 45.6% good question, 24.1% unsure, 28.3% bad question; ECE 0.13 experts vs 0.12 non-experts. No CIs or significance tests on model numbers; no clustering adjustment by writer/validator. Power admission: 448 items detect only ~50%->60% effects at 80% power. Cost: ~$95/hr average pay, $150/hr max (implying roughly $150-300 per finished question); no total spend reported.
implications: Power/scale answer for the question of record: GPQA admits 448 i.i.d. items resolve only ~10-point effects at 80% power, and its CIs ignore clustering over its 61 writers. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's 8 templates x ~18 instances has effective n ~= 8 for template-level claims because instances share failure modes. Report cluster-robust (by-template) CIs; to claim single-digit pass rates with ~+/-3-point 95% CIs, grow to ~25-40 independent templates with >=10 instances each plus k>=3 repeats per instance to separate decoding noise from item difficulty; use paired designs (same instance across models; clean-vs-defect within instance, McNemar) as GPQA recommends paired tests to rescue power at small n.

Make a prompt-ablation leakage probe a release gate, generalizing GPQA's answer-only baselines: GPQA required T5/CBOW answer-only classifiers to stay at chance before claiming 'no easy tells'. CRUCIBLE saturated at 94-100% exactly because prompts leaked method recipes and answer menus. Before release, evaluate frontier models on ablated prompts (data withheld / menu withheld / recipe sentences withheld) and require near-floor performance on each; note GPQA's own caveat that underpowered probes prove little (their probes also failed on SNLI-350), so probe with the strongest model, not a weak classifier.

Gate templates on measured frontier-model failure the way GPQA gates on non-expert failure, with an iterate-and-revise loop: since the deterministic generator already guarantees label correctness (GPQA spent ~$95/hr and 5 stages to reach only ~74% objectivity), spend the whole validation budget on difficulty - run candidates against 2-3 frontier models under the final harness, revise until clean-condition pass is under target, and tier releases like Extended/Main/Diamond with an elite subset that defeated all reference models.

Engineer attractive wrong paths from GPQA's writer strategies that produced 34% non-expert accuracy: use resolved controversies as distractor paths, encode implicit tacit practice (the correction a textbook recipe omits), disguise the domain so solvers cannot pattern-match a named method, add irrelevant information, and honor GPQA's 'minimal calculation' rule - difficulty must come from judgment calls, not arithmetic a tool can do.

Pre-register abstention/refusal scoring: GPQA shows handling can move headlines >10 points (GPT-4+search 28.2% raw at 37.2% abstention -> 39.4% with backoff; zero-shot GPT-4 abstains 26.2% vs few-shot 0.2%, confounding comparisons). Since CRUCIBLE's flawed-premise condition makes refusal correct, define machine-checkable refusal criteria per condition, report the full answer/refuse x clean/defect/flawed matrix per model, and forbid backoff/retry policies that blur conditions.

Use the generator for the contamination defense GPQA could not have: GPQA's defenses (canary string, plea not to repost, 18-item static held-out) are honor-system and tiny. Regenerate fresh instances with new seeds per evaluation campaign, keep live parameter ranges private, embed a canary GUID in every released file, and compare pass rates on released vs freshly generated instances - a divergence is a direct contamination measurement.

Buy a human baseline using GPQA's incentive playbook (correctness-conditional bonuses ~$30/question, ~$95/hr average, 15-min engagement floors, adjacency exclusions, AI-assistant ban, self-reported confidence enabling ECE, sufficient-expertise self-report): without an expert-vs-skilled-non-expert-vs-model triangulation like 65/34/39, a single-digit frontier pass rate is uninterpretable - it could mean hard, or broken. GPQA's Table 4 warns that even careful pipelines yield ~28% 'bad question' rates once humans probe them.

Report per-stage conditional pass rates, not just non-compensatory chain pass/fail: GPQA's domain heatmap, expertise gaps (delta 23.5-40.6 pts), and organic-vs-other-chemistry split (81% vs 55%) turned one accuracy number into diagnosis. Stage-level logging multiplies observations ~6x for power, localizes which trap defeats which model, and exposes degenerate templates where one stage does all the work.

Correct for selection effects when keeping only templates models fail: GPQA stars every filtered-subset human number as selection-skewed and brackets truth between filtered and unfiltered values. After selecting templates by frontier failure, re-estimate pass rates on newly generated instances of those templates (free with the generator) and report both selection-set and fresh-set numbers, mirroring extended-vs-main-vs-diamond.

read.n_items: 5,000 conversation examples (1-19 turns, mean 2.6; median 11 rubric criteria each, range 2-48; 48,562 unique criteria / 57,237 occurrences across 7 themes and 5 axes). Mostly synthetic conversations from an LLM pipeline seeded with physician-enumerated situation types, plus physician red-teaming and LLM-rewritten HealthSearchQA queries, filtered by o1-preview graders. Rubrics written by 262 physicians (26 specialties, 60 countries, 49 languages) over 11 months; example-specific criteria single-authored, 34 consensus criteria attached by majority vote (min 2 raters). Subsets: HealthBench Consensus = 3,671 examples / 34 criteria only; HealthBench Hard = 1,000 difficulty-selected examples (cross-provider 5-model screen, drop ~1.5% all-fail items, keep lowest mean score).
read.key_stats: Overall (0-1, 16-run mean/std): o3 0.5990/0.0016, GPT-4.1 0.4778/0.0022, o1 0.4200/0.0022, GPT-4o Aug24 0.3233/0.0020, GPT-3.5T 0.1554/0.0029 — no CIs or significance tests anywhere, only repeatability std ~0.002. HealthBench Hard: best model o3 = 0.32, many models score 0. Consensus subset: GPT-4.1 0.9398 down to GPT-3.5 0.7509 (error rates fell >4x), but context-seeking-when-context-missing criteria stay at 0.01-0.50 across all models. Human baseline: unassisted physicians scored below Sep-2024 models; physicians improved Sep-2024 references 56.2% vs worsened 39.8%, but Apr-2025 references only 46.8% vs 47.7% (arm sizes unreported). Judge agreement: GPT-4.1 grader macro F1 0.709 vs physician-physician 0.55-0.75; beats average physician in 5/7 themes (percentiles 37.5-88.2); grader spread 0.580-0.709 by judge model. Reliability: o3 worst-at-16 is one-third below its 0.60 mean. Length bias: o3 r=+0.123; length-controlled win rate o3>GPT-4.1 falls 72.9%->63.7%. Cost: GPT-4.1 nano beats GPT-4o Aug24 at 25x cheaper (no absolute dollar figures in text).
implications: Adopt HealthBench Hard's selection recipe for the next CRUCIBLE pool: oversample instances 3-5x, score with ~5 models across providers, rank by cross-provider MEAN score (not min, so difficulty is not vendor-adversarial) — but repurpose their all-models-fail filter (~1.5% dropped as rubric noise) as an AMBIGUITY detector, since CRUCIBLE labels are deterministic; and plan periodic re-selection because Hard decayed to 0.32 for o3 within one release cycle.

Scale answer for the question of record: HealthBench's 0.002 std comes from averaging ~55,000 graded continuous units per run; CRUCIBLE's binary all-stage-pass metric at target p~0.05 needs n~456 independent items for a 2pp 95% CI half-width (n~1,825 for 1pp), and with only 8 templates the effective n collapses to the cluster count — so target >=30 independent templates x >=15 instances (>=450 items), k>=4 seeds, and report template-cluster-robust CIs, which HealthBench never needed because every example is its own cluster.

Keep the non-compensatory chain-pass headline but also log per-stage binary results (CRUCIBLE's analogue of HealthBench's per-criterion grading and axes) for statistical power and failure attribution, and lift their worst-at-k machinery verbatim: N=16 samples per item, exhaustive subset-min averaging (unbiased U-statistic with min kernel, Clemencon et al. 2016) — o3 losing a third of its score from mean to worst-at-16 shows response-variance is an exploitable difficulty axis.

Report clean / planted-defect / flawed-premise as three separate headline numbers and up-weight flawed-premise: HealthBench Table 8 proves frontier models sit at 0.94-1.00 on accuracy strata while scoring 0.0166-0.5028 on 'seek context instead of answering' — the same recognize-when-not-to-answer behavioral class as CRUCIBLE's refusal-correct condition — and an aggregate hides a 90-point spread; also mine Appendix I's condition-flipped criteria structure (correct behavior inverts by category) as the template for attractive wrong paths.

Layer contamination defenses at the TEMPLATE level: copy the canary GUID + do-not-repost request + private held-out set, but since CRUCIBLE's saturation leak was method recipes and answer menus (template-level, not instance-level), keep 25-30% of templates fully private and publish the public-vs-private template-level score gap as a standing tripwire statistic with every release.

Any LLM-judged stage (refusal detection, free-text justification) needs HealthBench-style meta-evaluation before trust: labeled meta-eval set, per-criterion MACRO F1 (chosen for class imbalance — refusal detection is imbalanced too), a stated random baseline (0.50), judge-model sensitivity table (their spread 0.580-0.709 exceeds most model gaps), and tune the judge prompt on a different model family than those being ranked to avoid their GPT-4.1-tunes-GPT-4.1 circularity; prefer CRUCIBLE's deterministic scoring everywhere it is possible.

Run a scaffold-controlled paired analysis mirroring their length-control: every item in scaffolded (menus/recipe present) and bare form, same instances and models, report the per-model scaffold gap — this quantifies how much of v1's 94-100% saturation was prompt-leak artifact (their analogue: o3's win rate fell 72.9%->63.7% under length control) and doubles as the regression test that the redesign removed the leak.

Design the expert human baseline as framing-dependent evidence, not a gold ceiling: HealthBench physicians lost to 2024 models unassisted (partly brevity/framing artifacts, per-arm n never reported), so give humans the exact bare model prompt, equivalent tooling, pre-registered arm sizes with CIs, and consider a with-model-reference arm to test whether expert+model beats both alone in the science domain.
quotes: Abstract: "We present HealthBench, an open-source benchmark measuring the performance and safety of large language models in healthcare. HealthBench consists of 5,000 multi-turn conversations between a model and an individual user or healthcare professional."
Section 2 (Rubric evaluations): "Each rubric criterion has an associated nonzero point value between −10 and 10, with negative points used for criteria that are undesirable."

Section 1 (Introduction): "We establish human baselines where physicians were instructed to produce responses both with and without model assistance, finding that recent models produce higher quality responses than physicians unless physicians are assisted by the same models."

Section 6.4 (Reliability): "while o3 achieves a score of 60% on HealthBench overall, its worst-at-16 score is reduced by a third in comparison, indicating there are still many problems on which it is not fully reliable."

Section 8.1 (Meta-evaluation results): "It exceeds the average physician score in five out of seven themes, is in the upper half of physicians for six out of seven themes, and is above the lower third (33rd percentile) of physicians for all themes."
Section 8.2 (Variability): "We observe a standard deviation of around 0.002 for different models, for scores ranging from 0.16 to 0.60, indicating low overall variability."
Section 9 (Discussion): "Similarly, writing of example-specific criteria was done by individual physicians, and—other than consensus criteria—criteria were not validated by other physicians."

Section 12 (Code and data): "To enable us to identify instances of (accidental) training or implicit overfitting on HealthBench, we retain a small private held-out set of identically distributed HealthBench examples."

read.n_items: 2,500 public questions (76% exact-match, 24% multiple-choice with 5+ options; ~14% require an image; Math 41%, Bio/Med 11%, CS/AI 10%, Physics 9%, Humanities/SS 9%, Chemistry 7%, Engineering 4%, Other 9%), plus an unreported-size private held-out set and a second private set from post-release late contributions. Construction funnel: ~1,000 expert contributors (500+ institutions, 50 countries) incentivized by a $500K prize pool and co-authorship; 70,000 logged pre-submission attempts -> ~13,000 items that stumped a frozen frontier-LLM panel (exact-match had to stump all of GPT-4o/Gemini 1.5 Pro/Claude 3.5 Sonnet/o1 (+o1-mini, o1-preview text-only); MC all but one) -> 6,000 candidates after round-1 human review (1-3 graduate-level reviews each, 3-5 min, solution verification waived if >5 min) -> 2,500 approved in round 2 by organizers/trained reviewers; post-release bug bounty, Scale AI student solve-to-consensus audits, and a search-on/search-off searchability purge.
read.key_stats: Headline accuracy (Table 1, point estimates, single run): GPT-4o 2.7%, Grok 2 3.0%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 4.1%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 4.6%, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking 6.6%, o1 8.0%, DeepSeek-R1 8.5% (text-only), o3-mini(high) 13.4% (text-only); RMS calibration error 73-89% (all >70%). Category best: o3-mini(high) Math 18.6%, Physics 15.3%. Human baseline: none measured (no human test-takers; correctness rests on author solutions + review). NO confidence intervals, standard errors, significance tests, clustering, or repeats anywhere; mixed temperatures (0.0 configurable, o1/o3-mini forced 1.0, Gemini FT 0.7). Inter-rater/label noise: expert disagreement 15.4% on public set (two 200-question audit rounds with author rebuttal), ~18% on bio/chem/health subset, 25% under single-dissenting-reviewer rule (FutureHouse externally claimed ~30% of chem/bio answers likely wrong). Judge: o3-mini-2025-01-31 structured-decoding answer-equivalence judge (GPT-4o at submission stage) with no reported judge-human agreement rate. Cost disclosed: $500,000 prize pool ($5,000 x top 50, $500 x next 500); eval compute cost not reported. Authors forecast models plausibly >50% by end of 2025.
implications: Treat the template as the sampling/clustering unit and grow templates, not instances: HLE's 2,500 items work because they span ~1,000 independent authors and 100+ subjects; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's 8 templates x ~18 instances is effectively n=8 for generalization claims since instances share the leaked recipe. Separating 5% vs 10% pass rates (alpha=0.05, power 0.8) needs ~430 items/model under independence, and with within-template ICC 0.2-0.5 at 18 instances the design effect is ~4.4-9.5, so at 8 templates no instance count suffices. Target 30-50 independent templates, report cluster-robust or hierarchical-bootstrap CIs over templates, and add 3+ repeats at fixed decoding plus per-stage scoring (5-8 Bernoulli observations per item) to multiply power without abandoning the non-compensatory headline metric.

Adopt HLE's pre-submission difficulty gate generator-side with a frozen, documented model panel: HLE only accepted items stumping a named panel (exact-match: all models; MC: all but one) and logged 70,000 attempts to get 13,000 qualifiers; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN should calibrate each template's distractor gap and defect subtlety against a versioned frontier panel until clean-condition pass rates hit single digits, record panel versions (HLE Table 4 style), and pre-register a recalibration/rotation trigger, because panel-relative difficulty decays fast - HLE's own authors forecast >50% within a year and built HLE-Rolling as the migration path; a generator makes seed-rotation releases nearly free.

Fix the leakage channel HLE never faced - the prompt itself: HLE's defenses (originality rules, search-on/search-off audits, private split) target retrieval from the world, but CRUCIBLE-CHAIN saturated at 94-100% via in-prompt method recipes and answer menus. Strip procedural scaffolding from prompts, never enumerate candidate answers (prefer exact-match over MC - HLE is 76% exact-match and had to inflate MC option counts against lucky guessing; its reviewers noted models flip to correct when formatting help is added), keep a private seed split, and publish public-vs-private per-model deltas as the overfitting probe HLE promised but never reported numbers for.

Protect and advertise constructed truth with a published label-error audit: HLE's signal (2.7-13.4% accuracy) sits below its label-noise floor (15.4% public-set expert disagreement, ~18% bio/chem/health, 25% single-reviewer, ~30% claimed by FutureHouse), making small model differences uninterpretable and forcing a bug bounty plus rolling fork. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's near-zero label error is exactly what makes single-digit targets meaningful - but chains of judgment calls can reintroduce HLE-style ambiguity, so verify each stage's intended call is uniquely derivable from the given data (property-based tests plus independent generator reimplementation), replicate HLE's cheap audit protocol (2 x 200-item expert samples with author rebuttal), and publish the measured disagreement rate as a headline differentiator.

Score programmatically and validate any extraction step - HLE didn't: its o3-mini judge does genuine symbolic equivalence reasoning (the paper's own example proves a trig identity) with no reported judge-human agreement, and the judge changed between pipeline stages (GPT-4o -> o3-mini). At single-digit targets, judge error would dominate CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's measurement: use deterministic parsers with codified numeric tolerance; where free-text stage answers need extraction, copy HLE's narrow structured-extraction prompt (extract-and-compare only, judge forbidden from solving) and report extraction agreement on a hand-graded sample.

Make the flawed-premise condition ungameable and report an abstention/calibration table like HLE's: HLE's second headline (RMS calibration error >70% - models confabulate confidently rather than abstain) shows abstention metrics get cited alongside accuracy, but a model that learns refusal is sometimes right can refuse indiscriminately. Score conditions jointly per model - flag precision/recall on defect and flawed-premise conditions conditioned on high clean-condition accuracy so blanket refusal is dominated - and elicit per-stage verbalized confidence (HLE's Explanation/Answer/Confidence format) to publish a calibration number directly comparable to HLE Table 1.

Keep only the two human checks that survive automation: (a) an empirical attractive-wrong-path audit - HLE's round-2 rubric discards 'artificially difficult' or merely adversarial items; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's analog is confirming via baseline model runs that each stage's designed distractor is actually taken, since an untaken distractor adds length not difficulty; (b) a public bug-bounty window on template logic itself, because a single generator bug corrupts ~18 instances at once - HLE's per-item error blast radius was 1, a template's is a full cluster, the flip side of constructed truth.

Exceed HLE's statistical reporting as a positioning move: HLE reports zero CIs, no significance tests, single runs at inconsistent temperatures (0.0 vs forced 1.0 vs 0.7), and point estimates whose adjacent gaps (2.7 vs 3.0) are within +/-0.9pp binomial noise even at n=2,500; category cells carry several-point CIs unmentioned. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's question of record should be answered with pre-registered Wilson/cluster-bootstrap CIs, explicit repeat counts, and a power analysis in the paper - a differentiator no current frontier benchmark, including HLE, provides.

implications: Kill the answer menu: LAB-Bench's open-answer sidecar shows MCQ menus donate 2-3x score to strong models (CloningScenarios precision 0.54 MCQ vs 0.20 open-answer; both models solved the same 2/10 by guessing modal BsaI/Ampicillin). Since CRUCIBLE-CHAIN saturated partly via leaked answer menus, make every stage free-form and check against generator truth with a deterministic checker - avoid LAB-Bench's LLM fallback parser, which reintroduces the label noise constructed truth eliminates.

Audit and adversarially set answer marginals per template: models scored on LAB-Bench by guessing domain-modal answers; the generator should force flat correct-answer marginals across instances and plant the domain-modal choice as the attractive wrong path in a controlled fraction, so priors-only strategies score below chance - a control LAB-Bench lacked entirely.

Scale for significance with templates as the clustering unit: LAB-Bench's 41 clustered CloningScenarios with zero CIs/tests (only SD over 3 runs) is the cautionary tale (binomial 95% CI half-width ~0.14 at n=41). For single-digit-pass-rate claims: distinguishing 5% vs 10% at alpha=0.05/power 0.8 needs ~430 independent items; instances within a template are correlated, so grow from 8 to 25-40 independent templates, measure intraclass correlation in a pilot, inflate n by design effect 1+(m-1)ICC, report cluster-bootstrap CIs over templates, and run >=3 seeds per model to separate decode variance from item variance.

Use human proof-of-possibility, not a human baseline: LAB-Bench could not get a fair baseline on 10-60-minute tasks despite $50-100/hr incentive engineering (annotators skipped them; the 0.60 Cloning baseline is admittedly 'unreasonably low'). For 5-8-stage chains, record 1-2 documented expert walk-throughs per template with time-on-task, and use humans only for face-validity calibration review of the first few instances per new template - the generator is the label authority.

Score refusal as a first-class outcome with the accuracy/precision/coverage triple per condition: LAB-Bench's refusal option made accuracy and precision diverge wildly (Claude 3.5 Sonnet LitQA2: 0.06 accuracy vs 0.47 precision at 12% coverage) and tables silently report precision on ~4 attempted items. Define flawed-premise correct = refusal, and use the clean-control condition to catch indiscriminate refusers; never quote precision below a minimum attempt count; reuse LAB-Bench's 'unsure + best guess with EV >= random guessing' payout design if humans are run.

Contamination defense: adopt LAB-Bench's kit (canary string in every artifact, 20% private split, public-private gap monitoring - they observed <5% absolute) but exploit the generator: hold out seed space and regenerate fresh instances each evaluation round. Critically, LAB-Bench published its full distractor formulas in Appendix C, leaking the method even where items stayed private - CRUCIBLE-CHAIN saturated exactly via leaked method recipes, so the release policy must cover generator decision rules and defect taxonomies, not just item text.

Mine attractive wrong paths from the model 'null space': LAB-Bench found model-drafted nonsensical questions, once human-revised, are disproportionately hard for models, and its observed failure modes (recalling vs matching sequences, subsequence location, off-by-one fragment counting) map directly onto planted-defect design. Run frontier models on draft chains and instantiate their systematic mistakes as the planted defects, targeting single-digit pass rates empirically; chains requiring exact intermediate-quantity carry-forward were hardest for all models.

Verify difficulty survives surface-form changes: LAB-Bench tasks flipped from ~95% to ~60% precision when only the input encoding changed (sequence given vs gene name; Gibson-HindIII vs Gibson-SmaI variants diverged for no principled reason). Instantiate each CRUCIBLE-CHAIN template across surface variants and require within-template pass-rate stability - instability means the template measures format familiarity, the exact failure mode that let recipe leakage saturate v1.

read.n_items: No new benchmark items - this is a position/infrastructure paper (v3, 31 May 2026) distilling 3 years of maintaining lm-eval. Case studies re-run existing benchmarks: ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, and MMLU (57 subjects, micro-averaged) on 5 open-weight base models under 2 prompt styles each, 0-shot, lm-eval v0.4.2. Quoted sizes of others' benchmarks: HumanEval = 164 examples (variance warning); ARC has one 5-choice question among 4-choice; HumanEval has 3 documents missing example tests. lm-eval tasks are community-contributed YAML/Python configs matching the originating paper's methodology (or the first prompted adaptation, usually GPT-3).
read.key_stats: Prompt format alone moves scores 14-46pp and flips rankings (all 95% bootstrap CIs, 0-shot): ARC-C cloze vs MMLU-style - GPT-NeoX-20B 38.0+/-2.78 vs 26.6+/-2.53; Falcon-7B 40.2+/-2.81 vs 25.9+/-2.51; Mistral-7B 50.1+/-2.86 vs 72.4+/-2.56; Mixtral-8x7B 56.7+/-2.84 vs 81.3+/-2.23. MMLU hybrid vs MMLU-style: Mistral 48.3+/-0.80 vs 58.6+/-0.77; Mixtral 59.7+/-0.77 vs 67.1+/-0.72. Extreme case: GPT-NeoX ARC-Easy 72.4+/-1.80 (cloze) collapses to 26.5+/-1.78 (~chance) under MMLU-style. MMLU micro vs macro averaging shifts results "several percentage points". Borrowed GPQA figure (Lukosiute 2024): single-run point estimates vs 95% CIs over 10 runs reverse model orderings. Three independent MMLU implementations change ranking order (Fourrier 2023b). No human baseline, no judge, no significance tests performed in-paper; CIs are i.i.d. bootstrap (not clustered). Compute: 8x A40 48GB, under 1 day.
implications: Remove answer menus/recipe leaks and score free-form generation against the generator's truth: saturation at 94-100% is the paper's closed-domain-conversion failure mode (MMLU-style letter-matching rewards format compliance, +24.6pp for Mixtral). CRUCIBLE-CHAIN has the 'practical verifier' the paper calls rare (deterministic generator), so require free-form stage outputs checked mechanically with tolerance windows; diff each prompt against generator code and delete any token narrowing the judgment space.

Treat prompt phrasing as a measured variable: two legitimate phrasings move scores 14-46pp and flip rankings, so a single-digit pass-rate claim from one phrasing per template is fragile. Ship 2-3 registered paraphrase variants per template (PromptSource-style multiprompt evaluation), report the distribution, and state headline results as a range.

Answer the scale question with clustered uncertainty: calibration from the paper is ~1.2k items -> +/-2.8pp, ~14k items -> +/-0.7-0.8pp (95% CI). At p~0.05 with n=144, i.i.d. CI is ~+/-3.6pp (cannot separate 3% from 9%), and instances within a template are correlated, so effective n collapses toward 8 templates - too few for any significance claim. Grow independent templates to 30-50 (not instances per template), use cluster bootstrap over templates, and pre-register a power analysis targeting n_eff >= 300-500 for the claim of record.

Report both variance notions the paper distinguishes: bootstrap-over-items (new questions from the distribution) AND run-to-run decoding stochasticity (the 10-run GPQA figure). Non-compensatory 5-8 stage chains amplify sampling noise (~8x per-stage flip probability), so run 5-10 sampled repeats per item at deployment temperature and never claim model separation smaller than the across-run band.

Log per-stage per-sample artifacts and audit extraction before scaling: with menus gone, scoring depends on free-form extraction the paper calls 'highly imperfect' and format-biased; refusal detection in the flawed-premise condition is itself an extraction problem since refusal wording varies by model. Publish a Filter-style extraction pipeline, persist all outputs lm-eval --log_samples-style, and manually audit sampled chain failures per model to separate format compliance from answer correctness.

Version the benchmark like lm-eval versions tasks: the de-leaked CRUCIBLE-CHAIN is a new version (metadata.version pattern); publish exact prompts, generator code+seed, extraction code, and all model outputs per release; disclose prompt-engineering effort per condition; forbid comparing v1.0 saturated scores with v2.0 scores as the same benchmark.

Exploit the generator as a contamination/anti-gaming defense static benchmarks lack: the Benchmark Lottery shows idiosyncrasies down to separator tokens become fine-tuning targets once a benchmark matters. Mint fresh seed-rotated instances per evaluation, keep a public reproducibility split plus a private headline split and unpublished holdout templates, and report public/private deltas as a gaming indicator.

Protect construct validity with realistic framing and mandatory qualitative error analysis: the paper warns exam-style formats poorly predict deployment behavior and that loglikelihood vs generative framings disagree; keep scoring on artifacts a scientist would produce (estimates, flags, reasoned refusals), and include per-model failure categorization by stage type and condition (clean/planted-defect/flawed-premise) in each release report.

read.n_items: 1000 questions across 18 tasks in 6 categories (per-task n=36-100: thirteen tasks at 50, plot_unscrambling 40, olympiad 36, math_comp 96, LCB_generation 78, AMPS_Hard 100). Constructed by the author team via generator scripts over post-cutoff sources (AMC/AIME/SMC/USAMO/IMO 2023-24 with prose/answer-order/format modification, Guardian articles via API, Kaggle/Socrata datasets, arXiv abstracts with injected typos, IMDb synopses of 2024+ films, NYT Connections, LiveCodeBench April 2024) plus procedurally generated harder variants of BBH Web of Lies, Zebra puzzles (solver-verified unique solutions), AMPS, and IFEval-style instruction composition; 50 spatial questions handwritten. Refreshed monthly: 1/6 of questions replaced per update, newest month embargoed (always 1/6 private), generator code never released and always modified between refreshes.
read.key_stats: Top model o1-preview-2024-09-12 scores 64.7/100 ("6% better than all other models"); claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 58.5; o1-mini 56.7 (best reasoning 72.3); best open llama-3.1-405b 51.1; all 40 models below 70%. No human baseline anywhere. Uncertainty: 95% bootstrap CIs shown only graphically (Figures 1/5), no numeric CIs, no significance tests, single run at temperature 0. No LLM judge (deterministic regex/programmatic scoring); anti-judge ablation: GPT-4-Turbo judge error rates 10.3-46.0% on AMC12/AIME/SMC/Zebra, inflating weak scores (Zebra 38 ground-truth vs 68 LLM-judged). Correlation with ChatBot Arena 0.91, Arena-Hard 0.88; category-vs-overall Pearson r 0.82-0.95 (std err 0.05-0.08). Refresh stability: rank correlation >0.997 across monthly updates, mean score drift -1.2%. Cost for full 1000-question run: $0.90 (claude-3-haiku) to $53.80 (claude-3-opus); o1-preview $47.87; mean 1612 input / 395 output tokens per question.
implications: Report cluster-aware CIs and grow independent templates before instances: LiveBench needs ~1000 items over 18 heterogeneous tasks and still shows only graphical CIs with per-task std errors 0.05-0.15; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's 8 templates x ~18 instances is ~144 items but only 8 quasi-independent clusters, so bootstrap over templates (hierarchical: template then instance), and target ~18+ template families; at a true 5% pass rate a +/-2.5pp Wilson CI needs ~300 quasi-independent items (~18x18), and separating 3% vs 8% between frontier models needs ~250+ items plus paired McNemar-style tests (possible since all models see identical items - LiveBench never does this).

Treat generator and prompt scaffolding as private embargoed assets: LiveBench never releases generator code, always modifies the generator between refreshes, and embargoes 1/6 of questions monthly; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN saturated because prompts leaked method recipes and answer menus - strip method/menu scaffolding from prompts (raw data + question only, never the generator's option list), publish only spent instances, keep a never-published held-out instance set regenerated with fresh seeds per evaluation, and version the generator per release.

Build difficulty dials into every template and re-tune per release: LiveBench parameterizes hardness (olympiad masking 10/50/80% drives scores 96.8 to 36; zebra levels 10-20; red herrings 0-19; typo rate U(0.5,0.7)) and refreshes the currently easiest tasks first, holding top models in a 30-70% band with -1.2% drift and >0.997 rank correlation; give each CRUCIBLE-CHAIN template explicit knobs (defect subtlety, distance between correct path and attractive wrong path, chain length 5-8, red-herring count) and calibrate against 2-3 frontier models per release to hit single-digit pass rates without hand-authoring new templates.

Decouple parse failure from reasoning failure, because non-compensatory scoring multiplies the confound LiveBench documents: regex grading 'adds an instruction-following element' to every task, mitigated by maximally permissive parsers plus routine manual audits of incorrectly-labeled responses with re-scoring of all models after parser updates; in a 5-8 stage all-must-pass chain a 2% per-stage parse-failure rate fabricates 10-15% chain failure - fatal at single-digit signal - so use per-stage permissive extraction, log parse-failure separately from wrong-answer per stage, audit random samples of zero-scored chains per model, and publish the parse-failure rate alongside pass rate.

Never fall back to LLM judging, including for the flawed-premise/refusal condition: LiveBench measured 10.3-46.0% judge error on exactly the hard math/reasoning items where judging tempts, distorting both directions (Zebra 38 GT to 68 judged; AMC12 56 GT to 42.9 judged) - a +30pt inflation would destroy a single-digit headline claim; score refusal deterministically (structured proceed/flag-premise field matched against generator metadata), mirroring how LiveBench converted unjudgeable proofs into deterministic equation-reordering rather than judging proof text.

Adopt LiveBench's refresh-regression metrics to certify the post-leak regeneration: they validate each refresh with rank correlation across versions (>0.997) and mean-score drift (-1.2%); run the pre-leak model set on the regenerated CRUCIBLE-CHAIN suite and publish both numbers - preserved ranks with absolute scores falling from 94-100% to the target band is evidence the fix removed leakage rather than changed the construct.

Exploit the advantage LiveBench lacks - free instances - for repeats and a human ceiling: LiveBench is rate-limited by the real world (olympiad/math_comp updatable only yearly, spatial handwritten), runs each model once at temperature 0 leaving generation variance unmeasured, and has no human baseline; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's deterministic generator mints unlimited near-zero-label-error instances, so run k=3-5 seeds/repeats per template-condition cell to estimate within-model variance and fold it into CIs, run a small expert-human baseline (cheap to score with constructed truth) to anchor difficulty claims, and pre-compute token cost per model as in LiveBench Tables 15-16 ($0.90-$53.80 per 1000 single-turn questions) before committing to a ~4,860-chain campaign.

State the aggregation rule up front and report per-condition scores: LiveBench's headline is a mean of category means that silently weights an olympiad question ~4x an AMPS_Hard question, and the paper contains an internal inconsistency (Section 3.2 claims math_comp is the top overall correlate; Table 6 shows web_of_lies_v2 at 0.9136 vs 0.9035); CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's three conditions are structurally different measurements, so define the headline metric now (minimum across conditions or the reported triple), weight templates equally with instance counts documented, and machine-check in-text numbers against tables before release.

read.n_items: 75 Kaggle competitions (22 Low / 38 Medium / 15 High complexity) plus a 7-competition dev split. Manually curated funnel: 5,673 completed Kaggle competitions (Meta Kaggle) -> exclude Community Competitions -> 586 manually screened -> 75 selected against 9 criteria, each screened by at least 2 ML engineers at leading AI companies. Each competition hand-ported: description scraped, new train/test split built (default 10% of original train; grouped/temporal splits where needed, fidelity checked via sample-submission score parity), grading code re-implemented for local deterministic scoring against Kaggle Private-leaderboard medal thresholds.
read.key_stats: Headline (any-medal %, mean +/- SEM over seeds): o1-preview (AIDE, 16 seeds) 16.9 +/- 1.1; GPT-4o (AIDE, 36 seeds) 8.7 +/- 0.5; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (AIDE, 3 seeds) 7.6 +/- 1.8; Llama 3.1 405B (AIDE, 3 seeds) 3.0 +/- 1.0; GPT-4o MLAB 0.8 +/- 0.5; GPT-4o OpenHands 4.4 +/- 1.4. o1-preview: 98.4% made submission, 82.8% valid, 29.4% above median, 9.4% gold. pass@8 doubles o1-preview to 34.1%; GPT-4o pass@6 = 17.0 ~ o1-preview pass@1. Time: 8.7% @24h -> 11.8% @100h. Hardware invariant (CPU-only 9.1 +/- 1.0 vs 2xGPU 10.2 +/- 2.0). Human baseline = full Kaggle Private leaderboards with medal thresholds; only 9 humans ever medaled 75+ competitions; o1-preview averages 7 golds (Grandmaster needs 5, with caveats). Contamination: familiarity-performance Pearson r = -0.24 (p = 0.04); obfuscated descriptions 8.4 +/- 1.0 vs original 8.5 +/- 0.6 (10 seeds). Rules judge (GPT-4o-mini): flags up to 14.1% of medal runs, 100% false positives on human review; Dolos plagiarism all <60% similarity. No between-model significance tests; SEM over seeds only (fixed task set, no clustering). Cost: 1,800 GPU-hours per full run; o1-preview seed = 127.5M input + 15.0M output tokens.
implications: Count clusters, not instances, for the scale question of record: MLE-bench's +/-1.1pp SEM on 16.9% took 75 independent tasks x 16 seeds (~1,200 runs) and still ignores task-sampling uncertainty. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's 8 templates x ~18 instances is effectively an 8-cluster benchmark (instances share recipe and failure mode), so report template-level bootstrap/cluster-robust CIs now and grow to 50-75 independent templates (MLE-bench's 75 is a defensible precedent) before making frontier-separation claims; added instances only shrink within-cluster noise.

Pre-register the resource envelope and publish pass@k: MLE-bench scores double from pass@1 to pass@6-8 (16.9 -> 34.1%) and rise 8.7 -> 11.8% from 24h -> 100h, so 'single-digit frontier pass rate' is meaningless without fixed attempts/token/tool budgets. Define the CRUCIBLE-CHAIN headline as pass@1 under a stated budget, publish the pass@k curve with the Chen-style unbiased estimator, and run >=3 repeats everywhere with 10+ on headline configs (MLE-bench used 3 default, 16-36 for headline rows).

Make the obfuscation A/B a permanent condition - it is exactly the experiment for the 94-100% saturation post-mortem: MLE-bench manually stripped provenance from all 75 descriptions while keeping task-sufficient info and measured 8.5 +/- 0.6 vs 8.4 +/- 1.0 over 10 seeds. Ship a minimal-information prompt variant (no method recipes, no answer menus, free-form answers) beside the full prompt and report the per-template delta; 10 seeds sufficed there to see multi-point effects, but +/-1pp effects are invisible at that n.

Kill answer menus structurally the way MLE-bench's CSV rule does: agents must produce an open-ended artifact graded deterministically, and a rule forbids writing answers from world knowledge (enforced by log inspection). CRUCIBLE-CHAIN can go further because the generator is deterministic: require open-format per-stage outputs validated by the generator, regenerate instance data (fresh constants) per evaluation release so memorization and menu-matching are impossible by construction; keep refusal open-ended in the flawed-premise condition so it cannot be pattern-matched as a visible option.

Keep a hard human-anchored headline but report a ladder beneath it: MLE-bench's any-medal ceiling is calibrated to the best humans ever (9 people with 75+ medals) yet it also reports made-submission/valid/above-median/bronze-silver-gold plus complexity and category breakdowns (Tables 9-10). For CRUCIBLE-CHAIN, keep non-compensatory all-stages-pass as the 'medal' and add stages-correct distributions, first-failed-stage histograms, and per-condition (clean/planted/flawed) tables with SEs so single-digit scores remain decomposable and progress from 2% to 9% is measurable.

Design attractive wrong paths at the demonstrated frontier weaknesses: MLE-bench found agents 'struggle to debug issues and recover from missteps', fail to budget time/compute, underuse the validation server even when prompted, and score ~0% on post-2022 competitions and whole categories (image segmentation, object detection, LLM finetuning) while acing well-known recipes. Plant defects downstream of early commitments (forcing recovery), reward checking behavior, and lean on novel constructed tasks with no public recipe - the near-zero post-2022 result is direct evidence that recipe-free novelty is where pass rates collapse.

Calibrate any LLM screen against humans and publish false-positive rates: MLE-bench's GPT-4o-mini rules judge flagged up to 14.1% of medal-winning runs and every flag was a false positive on human review. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's deterministic grading keeps LLMs out of the score path, but any transcript screening (e.g., detecting recipe leakage or flawed-premise gaming) needs rubric -> mandatory human review of flags -> published flag and confirmed rates.

Ship a 'conditions of measurement' spec and version everything: MLE-bench mandates disclosure (model, scaffold, internet access, hardware, runtime, any solutions in prompts) and pins prompts (Fig. 8) and hyperparameters (Table 7), yet still has internal aggregate mismatches (Table 2 vs Table 9: MLAB 0.8 vs 1.3, OpenHands 4.4 vs 5.1; 500 nodes vs 2000 steps). CRUCIBLE-CHAIN should publish prompt hashes, generator version, instance seeds, and budgets with every reported number so the current saturation is traceable to a specific leaked prompt version and future claims are reproducible.
