read.n_items: 5,700 items = 100 questions randomly subsampled from each of all 57 MMLU subjects (cais/mmlu test split, 14,042 total). Not new questions: original MMLU items re-annotated with error labels by 14 author-experts using a hierarchical decision-tree protocol (Question Assessment: bad question clarity / bad options clarity; Ground Truth Verification: no correct answer / multiple correct answers / wrong ground truth; plus ok and expert tags). Annotators traced items to original sources via exact-match web search where possible; suggested corrections recorded but original text/labels left unmodified. Companion synthetic corpus LabelChaos (~264k corrupted items from 5-6 human-labelled QA datasets) built for fine-tuning error detectors.
read.key_stats: Headline: estimated 6.49% of MMLU questions erroneous (stratified over 57 subsets; raw 338/5,700 = 5.93%; no CI). Per-subset: Virology 57% erroneous (33% wrong ground truth), Logical Fallacies 26%, College Chemistry 25%, Professional Law 18%, Human Sexuality 17%; nine subsets 0%. Error-type totals: bad question clarity 2.47%, multiple correct 1.54%, wrong ground truth 1.42%, no correct answer 0.62%, bad options clarity 0.44%. Inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa, 3 annotators, only 5 error-heavy subjects): 0.64-0.96 all-type, 0.64-1.0 binary. Re-evaluation (HELM v1.3.0 predictions, EM, top-10 models) shows rank churn on 100-item subsets when restricting to correct-only items: Llama 3.1 405B Virology 0.57 (rank 16) -> 0.93 (rank 1); GPT-4 (0613) Human Sexuality 0.91 (5th) -> 0.43 (last); Gemini 1.5 Pro (001) Human Sexuality 0.37 (55) -> 0.94 (6). EM vs correct-ratio Pearson r = 0.33-0.54 across 10 models (no p-values). Automatic error detection (positive class "not ok", Recall/F1/F2): best prompting Claude 3 Opus few-shot CoT F2 40.29; best RAG Claude 3 Opus zero-shot Wikipedia F2 41.92 (recall 82.61-83.91, F1 ~28, near flag-everything); best overall fine-tuned Llama3-8B+LoRA on LabelChaos F2 44.75 (recall 56.58). Per-subject detection spread: Virology F2 up to 87.8 vs College Mathematics <=10.6. Human baseline: none (annotators are gold). Uncertainty: NO error bars, CIs, or significance tests anywhere - authors state repeated runs "would have exceeded our funding capabilities". Cost: not in dollars; fine-tuning on one A100 40GB. Contamination: no defenses; paper infers memorisation from models matching wrong gold labels on erroneous Professional Law/Formal Logic items.
implications: Non-compensatory chains multiply label error, vindicating constructed truth and setting a brutal QC budget: MMLU's measured 6.49% per-question error rate, applied per stage, would corrupt ~33% of 6-stage all-must-pass items (1-0.9351^6); even 1% per-stage error corrupts ~6% of items - the entire single-digit target pass-rate budget. Keep every stage key generator-computed, and hold any hand-authored component (refusal rubrics, prompt frames) to <<1% error via a Redux-style audit with 2+ raters and reported kappa.

Run MMLU-Redux's correct-subset re-ranking test on CRUCIBLE-CHAIN itself: flagging 9-57 items per 100 reordered frontier models by 10+ rank positions (Llama 405B Virology 16th->1st; GPT-4 Human Sexuality 5th->last). With 8 templates x ~18 instances, each template is a 100-item-scale subset; publish per-item results and recompute the leaderboard under leave-one-template-out and deletion of any 6% of items - if rankings flip, the benchmark is under-powered at that scale (a concrete acceptance criterion for the scale question of record).

Scale answer: grow independent templates (clusters), not instances per template, and report cluster-robust CIs - the statistics MMLU-Redux omitted (no error bars, single runs, funding-limited) and whose absence undermines its rank-change claims. Instances sharing a recipe collapse effective n toward the template count (design effect 1+(m-1)*ICC; 144 items can carry ~8-40 effective observations); distinguishing 5% vs 10% pass rates needs ~400+ effective items per condition (alpha 0.05, power 0.8), so target 30-50+ independent templates, use stratified estimation across templates for headline numbers, and attach template-level bootstrap CIs plus repeats to every claim.

The saturation-by-leakage failure is the mirror image of MMLU's scaffolding errors (options split, correct Option E dropped, instruction lines lost, abbreviations defined only in neighboring textbook questions): audit the artifact around the task. Adapt the paper's Fig. 2 decision-tree protocol into a per-instance prompt audit - does the prompt name/imply any stage's method, enumerate an answer menu, disambiguate the judgment call, or make the flawed premise undetectable? Two auditors + kappa on a sample suffices: MMLU-Redux achieved kappa 0.64-0.96 with a simple flowchart.

Flawed-premise/refusal conditions inherit MMLU's hardest and least reliable error class: unspecified context and unanswerable-question judgments (lowest kappa 0.64 on the subset with subjective items; Global Facts had authoritative sources conflicting). For every flawed-premise instance, have the generator emit a machine-checkable defect witness (the specific inconsistency and minimal evidence chain), human-verify on a sample that the defect is detectable in principle from the prompt as shown, and timestamp any world-facing constants (copying the paper's praised 'as of 2020' practice) so instances don't rot into ambiguity.

Do not rely on LLM-based QC or judging: the best automated error detector managed only F2 44.75 (a fine-tuned 8B beating all frontier prompting), frontier RAG reached F2 ~42 only via degenerate flag-everything recall (83.91 recall, ~28 F1), and detection quality tracked error grossness not subtlety (Virology F2 87.8 vs College Mathematics <=10.6). CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's subtle planted defects sit at the College-Math end, so LLM validators will miss them - QC must be generator-side assertions plus human audit; if any stage needs free-text grading, benchmark the grader per template and consider a small fine-tuned grader over frontier prompting.

Use the defect conditions as a built-in contamination assay and regenerate to keep it live: MMLU-Redux could only infer memorisation post hoc (models reproducing WRONG gold labels on Professional Law/Formal Logic erroneous items, with no way to decontaminate a static scrape). CRUCIBLE-CHAIN can measure shortcut/memorisation directly - report per-model clean-vs-planted-defect and clean-vs-flawed-premise gaps as first-class metrics, and regenerate instance parameters per evaluation campaign since the deterministic generator makes fresh-instance evaluation nearly free.

Versioning, per-item transparency, and an errata protocol are part of credibility: MMLU-Pro silently inherited MMLU's errors, while MMLU-Redux ships a datasheet, Croissant metadata, git-hash-pinned versions, a Zenodo mirror, and a structured [ADD]/[FIX] community-correction workflow. Pin every CRUCIBLE-CHAIN leaderboard claim to a dataset version hash, publish per-item per-stage outcomes for third-party Redux-style re-analysis, and freeze item sets and scoring before model runs - the paper proves post-hoc item filtering alone can reorder a leaderboard.

read.n_items: 20 papers (ICML 2024 Spotlight/Oral, chosen via 8 automated GPT-4o filters then manual read; 42 authors contacted, 20 secured) decomposed into 8,316 binary-gradable leaf nodes (94-2,551 nodes per paper) in hierarchical weighted rubrics drafted by two OpenAI research engineers and co-developed/signed off by an original author of each paper (multiple weeks, many tens of hours each); plus 2 NeurIPS 2024 workshop dev papers, an internal held-out set, and JudgeEval (human-gold-labeled graded submissions for 5 papers)
read.key_stats: Best agent: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) BasicAgent 21.0+/-0.8% avg Replication Score (error = 1 SEM over 3 seeds); o1 BasicAgent 13.2+/-0.3, o1 IterativeAgent 24.4+/-0.7 (26.0+/-0.3 at 36h); o3-mini 2.6+/-0.2, GPT-4o 4.1+/-0.1, Gemini 2.0 Flash 3.2+/-0.2, DeepSeek-R1 6.0+/-0.3; scaffold flip: Claude drops to 16.1+/-0.1 under IterativeAgent. Code-Dev variant: o1 43.4+/-0.8 (correlation with full PB only r=0.48). Human baseline: 8 ML PhDs, 3 attempts/paper, best@3 = 41.4% at 48h vs o1 26.6% on 3-paper subset; humans overtake after 24h. Stratified: all models ~0-1.4% on Result Match vs 35-43% Code Dev; humans 72.4/20.4/8.9. Judge: o3-mini SimpleJudge F1 0.83 vs human gold labels (0.72 CodeDev/0.82 Execution/0.94 ResultMatch) at $66/paper; o1 0.84 at $830; human grading est. 12h/$1,200. No CIs, no significance tests, no clustering by paper, no inter-human agreement reported. Cost ~$400/paper o1 rollout = $8k/full run; 646 runs, 10 disqualified for blacklist use; agent reproduce.sh scripts averaged 5.5 min runtime.
implications: Hide the grading spec from candidates: PaperBench never shows the rubric to the agent (explicitly 'to prevent overfitting to the evaluation criteria') and keeps a separate judge-only addendum. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN saturated because prompts leaked method recipes and answer menus - move all stage criteria and answer spaces into grader-only artifacts and add a pre-release leakage grep over candidate-visible text, analogous to PaperBench's blacklist monitor.

Scale independent templates, not instances: PaperBench defends n=20 papers by counting 8,316 leaves, but that defense relies on compensatory weighted averaging; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's non-compensatory scoring makes each instance one Bernoulli trial and instances within a template are correlated, so effective n is currently 8 clusters. For significance (e.g., distinguishing 10% vs 30% at alpha=0.05, power 0.8, ~60+ independent items/condition), target roughly 25-40 independent templates x 6-10 instances x >=3 repeats per model, and report template-clustered SEM/CIs - the clustering PaperBench visibly omits despite per-paper run variance like 0.448/0.229/0.098.

Keep the non-compensatory headline but publish a stage-stratified diagnostic table: PaperBench's partial credit (added so 'agent performance improves incrementally') yields a 21% headline while true end-to-end Result Match is ~0-1.4% for every model, buried in Appendix I Table 9. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN should emit the per-stage pass ledger (free, since the generator knows stage truth) as a secondary table to locate chain breaks and verify each attractive wrong path actually attracts, without inflating the headline pass rate.

Build a JudgeEval-equivalent for any non-deterministic grading layer: PaperBench validated its judge on human-gold-labeled submissions and still only reached F1 0.83 (0.72 on the dominant code-correctness category), with no propagation of judge error into headline uncertainty. If CRUCIBLE-CHAIN uses an LLM anywhere (e.g., grading refusal justifications in the flawed-premise condition, or parsing free-text answers into stage values), hand-grade a gold transcript sample, report agreement, and re-validate on every judge-model change; audit even the deterministic extraction layer.

Freeze a private held-out template set as a saturation canary: PaperBench releases 2 dev papers and keeps a held-out set internal precisely because public author codebases create future contamination. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's constructed truth defeats pretraining contamination, but the recipe-leakage failure mode recurs at release time - keep unreleased templates with novel trap structures private and monitor the public-vs-held-out score gap after each release.

Report multi-scaffold results before claiming single-digit frontier pass rates: PaperBench's model ranking inverted across two scaffolds (Claude 21.0->16.1, o1 13.2->24.4, 'highlighting models' sensitivities to prompting'), and forcing full time use doubled o1's score. Run each model under >=2 prompt framings and report the max, so a single-digit claim is not a harness artifact; if a framing change lifts scores dramatically, the prompts are leaking structure again.

Include a symmetric human solvability baseline: PaperBench's 8-PhD baseline anchors 'models do not yet outperform humans' but compares human best@3 at 48h to o1 mean at 36h with AI assistants allowed - asymmetries that blunt the claim. For a benchmark targeting single-digit model scores, blinded expert attempts on a sample per condition are needed to prove tasks are solvable-in-principle; report mean@k and best@k identically for humans and models, plus PaperBench-style operational hygiene (timesheets/snapshots, disqualification marks, infrastructure-failure disclosure).

Spend the grading-cost savings on rollouts and repeats: PaperBench pays $8k/run plus $66/paper judging and had to invent Code-Dev (only r=0.48 with the real benchmark) and pruned-rubric grading, where collapsing to one holistic judgment inflated a 0.25 score to 0.93. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's deterministic scoring is ~free, so budget goes to more templates x >=3 repeats per model-condition-instance cell; never replace stage-wise deterministic checks with a single holistic LLM judgment - Appendix H shows exactly where that decouples from truth.

read.n_items: 7 hand-crafted, novel, open-ended ML research-engineering environments (V1), each an 8-hour GPU-backed optimization run (0-6 H100s), authored by METR staff via a three-gate pipeline (specification review -> implementation + internal reference solution -> human baselining with adjustments); >12 specifications and >5 completed implementations were dropped in construction. Paired with 71 8-hour baseline runs by 61 human experts (45 runs from METR job applicants, 17 from professional networks incl. DeepMind/Google/Anthropic/OpenAI alumni, 9 from Berkeley/CMU/Stanford/MIT PhD students). Each environment ships a runnable scoring function with timestamped score log, a weak starting solution (normalized 0), and a hidden author reference solution (normalized 1); score = best log entry except Scaling Law (final submission only).
read.key_stats: Headline: best agents (o1-preview in AIDE; claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 in METR Modular) score 4x humans at a 2h total budget; humans narrowly exceed agents at 8h and reach 2x the top agent at 32h (best-of-k); best agents = 36th-37th percentile of the 71 human expert runs at 8h best-of-k. Human baseline: 82% of 71 expert attempts non-zero, 24% match/exceed reference solutions; source-stratified averages 0.98 (professional network) / 0.83 (grad students) / 0.48 (hiring applicants), pooled 0.64. Uncertainty: 95% CIs via percentile bootstrapping only (shaded bands, no numeric CIs in text; authors note downward skew from long right tail + best-of-k); no significance tests, no clustered errors. Judge: only Finetune GPT-2 for QA uses an LLM judge (llama-3-8b-instruct pairwise winrate); no judge-agreement stats reported; that environment has starting-score SD 0.62 and the best agent score fell 0.88 -> 0.69 on rerun (noise overfitting). Other key numbers: agents run the scorer 36.8/hr (AIDE) and 25.3/hr (Modular) vs 3.4/hr for humans; k=128 30-min samples still far below top human; engineering complexity (LOC) vs human-AI gap R^2=0.602; o1-preview kernel 0.64ms beats all 9 human experts. Cost: ~$123 per agent 8h run (~29M input + ~499K output tokens) vs ~$1,855 average human payment; validation gates: >70% of experts score >0.05 by 8h and >80% report score matched expectation in every environment; major technical issues in >5% of runs.
implications: Prove feasibility per template with a machine-checkable solvability certificate: RE-Bench requires >70% expert progress and >80% expectation-match per environment before trusting difficulty claims, citing SWE-bench's impossible items as the canonical failure. After CRUCIBLE-CHAIN strips recipe/menu leaks, re-derive each generator answer using only the model-visible artifact plus run a small expert/tool-assisted baseline per hardened template - otherwise a 6% frontier pass rate is indistinguishable from 6% answerable instances. Adopt their tri-gate pipeline (spec review -> implementation review -> baselining) and budget for RE-Bench-scale attrition (>12 specs, >5 finished implementations dropped to ship 7).

Answer the scale question in templates, not instances, with cluster bootstrap: RE-Bench's confessed weakness is n=7 environments making estimates 'sensitive to sampling noise' with wide skewed bootstrap CIs. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's ~18 instances per template share a recipe and failure mode, so effective n ~ 8 templates. Report percentile-bootstrap CIs resampling templates (clusters); measure intra-template correlation (ICC) in the pilot and publish design-effect-adjusted n; to separate models at 3-10% pass rates with 95% CIs you need several hundred effectively-independent items, i.e., grow to 30-60+ independent templates - adding instances to the existing 8 templates buys almost nothing.

Set and prove a guessing floor far below single digits per chain: RE-Bench's Scaling Law environment let random guessing score 0.99 and they prescribe ensuring 'random guessing did much worse than real solutions'. Compute the analytic guess-through probability per template (product over 5-8 stages of chance-picking the right branch given visible option space) and require <0.5%; a chain of binary judgment calls passes ~0.8% by pure luck at 7 stages, polluting single-digit measurements. Also run a no-content ablation agent (scaffolding without science content) as an empirical floor and leak probe.

Never expose scored signals during a run and instrument best-of-k gaming: RE-Bench agents exercised the scorer 25-37x/hour vs 3.4 for humans, rode evaluation noise to inflated bests (0.88 -> 0.69 on rerun), and METR now plans to hide test scores. For CRUCIBLE-CHAIN: no per-stage correctness feedback pre-submission; headline pass@1 at a pre-declared sampling policy with pass@k reported separately; regenerate a fresh instance from the same template for any top-scoring run to detect noise-riding - free with a deterministic generator, which RE-Bench lacked.

Automate right-for-wrong-reasons and exploit detection: RE-Bench caught o1-preview copying the reference model only by manually reading the top 2-15 transcripts per environment, leaving the mid-tail unaudited while score@k consumed the whole distribution. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's constructed truth knows every stage's intermediate value: require models to emit stage intermediates, score them mechanically, flag correct-final/wrong-intermediate runs, and for planted-defect instances have the generator emit tell-tale checks whose values differ under shortcut vs legitimate paths.

Measure lure uptake as a first-class metric: RE-Bench found 84% of Restricted-MLM attempts took the doomed attractive default (transformer tweaks) and agents polish starting solutions into local optima - direct validation of the attractive-wrong-path design. Report per stage and per model the fraction of failures that took the designed lure vs failed idiosyncratically: high uptake proves difficulty is judgment; low uptake with high failure signals ambiguity/noise, a feasibility defect masquerading as difficulty.

Ship detectability certificates for flawed-premise (refusal-correct) items per RE-Bench footnote 3: they demand unambiguous feasible tasks but concede ambiguity-testing evaluations need to 'ensure and demonstrate that the correct interpretation can be determined with sufficient skill and effort'. Have the generator name the specific inconsistency and the minimal observation subset revealing it, verify derivability from the model-visible artifact by script, and price false refusals against clean controls so a refuse-everything policy scores ~0.

Anchor 'hard' claims to stratified baselines, not pooled averages: RE-Bench's pooled percentiles blur a 2x gap between hiring applicants (0.48) and professional-network experts (0.98), and the paper itself warns against average-human comparisons. Publish CRUCIBLE-CHAIN results per-condition and per-template with a domain-stratified expert baseline on sampled instances; a pooled 6% hiding one saturated template plus seven at zero (RE-Bench's Scaling Law situation) has different meaning and variance than a uniform 6%.

read.n_items: 80 main problems decomposed into 338 subproblems across 5 fields / 16 natural-science subfields (physics 46% of mains); split 65 main / 288 sub test + 15 main / 50 sub dev; median 3 subproblems per main, max 15. Hand-authored by ~18 scientist co-authors (PhD-level+) from their own everyday research scripts (seldom open-sourced, some from unpublished manuscripts) plus Nobel-winning methods (DFT SCF, PMNS, Haldane model, optical tweezers, spin-glass replica). Three-round validation: >=2 in-domain scientists, 1 out-of-domain scientist, then GPT-4 generation with error analysis to redesign tests against false positives. Scoring is execution-based pass@1 (numerical I/O tests + domain-specific tests reproducing published results); main problem passes only if ALL subproblems and the integrated solution pass (non-compensatory). No LLM judge, no human baseline.
read.key_stats: Standard setup (no background, generated solutions carried over), pass@1 subproblem/main: Claude3.5-Sonnet 26.0%/4.6% (best), GPT-4o 25.0%/1.5%, GPT-4-Turbo 22.9%/1.5%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 21.9%/1.5%, Claude3-Opus 21.5%/1.5%, Deepseek-Coder-v2 21.2%/3.1% (best open), Llama-3-70B and Mixtral-8x22B 0.0% main. With scientist-written background: Claude3.5-Sonnet 35.4%/12.3%, GPT-4o 35.4%/9.2%; background deltas +4.5 to +10.8 (sub), +1.5 to +7.7 (main). Gold-conditioning curve improves to ~9 prior steps then declines (long context); dip at 7. CodeLlama-7B-Instruct 0.4%. NO confidence intervals, no repeats, no significance tests, no inter-rater agreement numbers, no human baseline, no cost or decoding params reported; on 65 test mains the percentages are raw counts (1.5%=1, 3.1%=2, 4.6%=3, 12.3%=8 problems), so headline model gaps (3 vs 1 successes) are statistically unresolved (Wilson 95% CI for 3/65 approx [1.6%, 13%]).
implications: Scale: SciCode's 65 test chains make every main-problem score a count of 0-8 successes, so its headline ranking (4.6% vs 1.5% = 3 vs 1 problems) is statistically unresolved. For single-digit pass-rate targets, distinguishing e.g. 4% vs 10% at alpha=0.05/power 0.8 needs ~300-450 independent items - and with 8 templates x 18 instances, within-template correlation makes the effective n closer to the template count. Grow to >=30 independent templates before adding instances, report by-template cluster-bootstrap CIs, and use paired McNemar tests on shared instances for model-vs-model claims.

De-saturation lever: SciCode's 'standard setup' deliberately withholds the scientist-written method background, and providing it moves main pass 4.6%->12.3% (+7.7) and subproblem pass +9 to +11 points - a direct measurement of what recipe leakage is worth. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN saturated (94-100%) precisely because prompts leaked method recipes and answer menus: make recipe-free prompts the scored condition (no method names, no formula menus, no enumerated answer options; require the model to state its own method choice as gradable output), and keep a recipe-provided condition as a diagnostic toggle whose delta is published as the benchmark's leakage value.

Chain compression is weaker than p^s because stage successes correlate: SciCode gets 4.6% main from 26% subproblem pass at median only 3 stages (naive independence predicts 1.8%; knowing the topic carries all stages). 5-8 stage chains will not automatically yield single-digit frontier rates: audit per-template stage-pass correlations from the saturation logs and redesign stages so each hinges on a different judgment type (method selection, defect detection, unit/convention choice, premise audit), verifying in pilots that each stage's attractive wrong path is actually taken.

Carry-over design: adopt SciCode's two-mode harness - generated-solutions-carried-forward as the primary scored metric (realistic, includes error accumulation) plus a gold-prefix-conditioned ablation (their Fig 3) reporting stage-conditional pass by depth to localize which stage kills chains. SciCode found degradation from long context only beyond 9 prior steps, so 5-8 stage chains are below that cliff and failures can be attributed to judgment rather than context management - state this explicitly when defending the design.

False-positive auditing: SciCode's third validation round ran GPT-4 on every problem and redesigned numerical tests to prevent false positives - but using one model family biased difficulty tuning against it. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN should red-team its graders with >=3 frontier families, manually audit every PASS in planted-defect and flawed-premise conditions for wrong-reason successes (answer-menu guesses, default-parameter flukes), require defects to be named/quantified rather than only reflected in a final number, and symmetrically audit refusal-correct items so blanket-refusal heuristics don't score as competence.

Contamination: SciCode's defense ('zero overlap with publicly available datasets', problems from unpublished internal scripts) is curation-time-only and decayed the day the dataset was released with gold solutions and tests. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's deterministic generator is structurally stronger - exploit it: release the generator and a frozen dev split only, keep test seeds private, regenerate fresh test instances (new parameter draws and defect placements) each leaderboard cycle with logged seeds for audit. Also version difficulty changes explicitly instead of SciCode's footnote-2 practice of quietly simplifying problems during revision.

Missing baselines to add: SciCode has no human baseline (research-level difficulty is asserted via provenance, never demonstrated) and no uncertainty reporting, decoding parameters, or cost - the two gaps a skeptic will probe on any 'frontier models fail' claim. Run 2-3 domain-competent humans on a stratified subsample (~1-2 instances per template, all three conditions, verifying experts do refuse on flawed premises), pre-register k>=3 repeats per item at fixed temperature, and publish mean pass rates with cluster CIs plus full decoding config and per-run cost.

read.n_items: 102 code-generation tasks adapted from 44 peer-reviewed publications / 31 GitHub repos across 4 disciplines (Bioinformatics, Computational Chemistry, Geographical Information Science, Psychology & Cognitive Neuroscience). Built by 9 graduate-student annotators who adapted published open-source programs into self-contained tasks (instruction + dataset info + optional expert knowledge + annotated gold program + executable success criteria + GPT-4o-drafted, expert-revised 5-stage rubrics). Funnel: 110 gathered -> 4 dropped (runtime/env) -> 106 -> expert validation by 9 subject-matter experts (revised 41 instructions, dropped 3) -> 103 -> non-author annotator cross-verification with reproduction runs (refined 29, dropped 1 for randomness) -> 102 final. Contamination/shortcut defenses: delete 5 random test points per dataset (fails memorized auto-loaders; skipped where it breaks data), and re-split + dummy test labels (-1) for model-development tasks.
read.key_stats: Headline (best-of-3 runs, selection on SR then VER/CBS/cost): Claude-3.5-Sonnet self-debug 32.4% SR without expert knowledge, 34.3% with; OpenAI o1-preview self-debug 42.2%/41.2% at >10x cost ($0.636-0.713/task vs $0.057-0.061); Claude OpenHands CodeAct 21.6%/24.5% at $0.958/task (self-debug +10.8 SR at 1/17th cost); direct-prompting Claude 17.7%/21.6% (text says 16.7/20.6 - internal inconsistency). Mean-of-3 +/- SD (Appendix E.1): Claude self-debug 22.9 (2.0) / 27.8 (2.0); o1 self-debug 27.1 (1.2) / 27.8 (1.7) - i.e., best-of-3 headline is ~5-10 points above the mean. No CIs, no significance tests, no clustering by the 44 source publications. Human baseline: none for task success; only annotation effort (>=2.5-3 h/task to adapt code vs ~10 min agent draft). Judges: GPT-4o figure judge (threshold >=60, 3 samples averaged), human-agreement asserted by citation only; rubric human eval = 2 raters averaged, no inter-rater kappa reported. Error analysis (Claude, 50 trajectories/framework): 29-30/50 semantic errors, 9-10/50 environment-config errors. Gold programs mean 58.6 lines; >75% of solved tasks below mean.
implications: Make mean-of-k the number of record and pre-register the aggregation rule: SAB's best-of-3 headline (32.4%) sits ~10 points above its own mean-of-3 (22.9%) because run selection uses the scoring metric itself, and its prose/table drift (16.7 vs 17.7) shows numbers must be generated from the results table, not hand-copied. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN should report mean pass over >=3 repeats with CIs and label best-of-k separately as pass@k.

Answer the scale question in independent templates, not instances: SAB's n=102 gives ~+/-9-point 95% binomial CIs and its 102 tasks cluster into 44 publications with no cluster adjustment; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's 8 templates are only 8 clusters (~7 df), so template-bootstrap CIs are currently uninformative. To separate single-digit rates (e.g., 4% vs 10%, alpha=0.05, power 0.8) plan ~250-350 effectively independent items per condition, i.e., >=30 independent templates x ~10-15 instances, with template-level bootstrap CIs as the reported uncertainty.

Keep method recipes out of the base prompt and make hints a separately-scored condition with written anti-leak rules: SAB keeps instructions deliberately concise, moves hints to an optional expert-knowledge condition with explicit anti-leak guidance ('documentation not code lines', ranges not exact values), and hints bought only +1.9 SR for the best agent while often hurting VER. Since CRUCIBLE-CHAIN saturated precisely via leaked recipes and answer menus, audit every prompt against a leakage rubric (no stage procedures, no candidate-answer enumerations) and score bare vs hinted conditions separately.

Certify deleaking with shortcut canaries and a no-data ablation: SAB's perturbations (delete 5 test points; dummy labels) exist to make memorized loaders and label-copying visibly fail, and Appendix F.4 shows one catching DeepPurpose's auto-loader. Each CRUCIBLE-CHAIN release should (a) run frontier models with the prompt but data withheld - above-chance scores prove prompt-side leakage; (b) plant instances whose correct answer contradicts the template's modal answer so recipe-following without data fails; (c) verify defect/flawed-premise instances flip the correct output vs the clean control under the same surface prompt.

Log per-stage outcomes even under non-compensatory scoring: SAB's 5-stage rubric evaluation found all discrimination in early stages (data loading/processing; 25% of failed programs scored <50 on loading) and none in output formatting/saving. Recording first-failing-stage per run identifies which 'attractive wrong path' actually attracts, exposes dead-weight stages to prune, and yields diagnostics without weakening the all-stages-must-pass headline metric.

Stay fully deterministic in scoring and cite SAB's figure judge as the anti-pattern: SAB is programmatic wherever possible (executable criteria, math.isclose, thresholds set by 5 gold-program runs) but falls back to a GPT-4o judge for figures with an unjustified >=60 threshold, no in-paper human-agreement number, and the judge doubling as an evaluated model. CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's constructed-truth generator makes every stage computable - keep LLM judges out of the scoring path entirely, and verify generator determinism the way SAB verified thresholds (N re-runs from spec, identical answers, stated as evidence).

Adopt SAB's two-stage independent verification and extend it for the refusal condition: expert questionnaire plus non-author re-execution caught defects at high incidence (41/106 instructions revised, 4 tasks dropped). For CRUCIBLE-CHAIN, each template needs a non-author reviewer who re-derives one instance's full chain by hand, and flawed-premise instances need a blinded reviewer to independently flag the premise - proving refusal is discoverably correct - plus false-refusal monitoring on clean controls. SAB has no refusal-correct condition, so this remains CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's differentiator to validate carefully.

Report cost as a first-class metric when recommending scale: SAB's cost column changed its conclusions (self-debug beats OpenHands at 1/17th cost; o1's +10 SR costs >10x), and the recommended CRUCIBLE-CHAIN scale-up (>=30 templates x ~12 instances x 3 conditions x >=3 repeats x several models ~ 30k+ runs) should be budgeted with per-run cost logs and a dollars-to-statistically-separate-two-models figure as part of the answer to the sponsor's scale question.

read.n_items: 2,294 test instances mined (not authored) from 12 popular Python repos: 93,139 crawled PRs -> attribute filter (merged PR + resolves linked issue + edits test files) -> 11,407 candidates -> execution-based validation (installs cleanly, >=1 fail-to-pass test, no import-artifact errors, no tests calling gold-patch-invented names) -> 2,294 (~2.5% yield; validation alone removes ~half). Plus 300-instance Lite subset, 225-instance dev set (6 disjoint repos), and 19,000-pair training set (37 disjoint repos). Gold labels = real merged human PRs; no crowdworkers, no human review pass over instance quality.
read.key_stats: Headline (BM25 retrieval, full 2,294): Claude 2 1.96% resolved (v3 adds Claude 3 Opus 3.79%, GPT-4-turbo 1.31%, ChatGPT-3.5 0.17%, SWE-Llama 7b/13b 0.70%). Oracle retrieval: Claude 2 4.80%, SWE-Llama 13b 3.97%; oracle-collapsed: Opus 9.39%, Claude 2 5.93%, GPT-4 3.40%. More BM25 context hurts (Claude 2: 1.96/1.87/1.22 at 13k/27k/50k). Temporal anti-contamination check: before/after-2023 flat (Claude 2 4.87 vs 4.23). Of Claude 2's 1,078 applied oracle patches, only 110 resolved; 471 No-Op, 436 Regression. NO confidence intervals, significance tests, or clustering anywhere; single greedy sample (pass@1); GPT-4 run on 25% subset (574 items) for budget. Scoring is deterministic execution (all fail-to-pass AND pass-to-pass tests must pass) — no LLM judge, no inter-rater stats, and NO human baseline (human solvability true by construction only). API cost unstated; SWE-Llama training 20h/4xA100 and 47h/8xA100.
implications: Size from the CI you need and cluster by template: SWE-bench's 1.96% on n=2,294 has an unreported ~±0.5pt Wilson CI and its per-repo cells (n=11-850) are noise; CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's 8 templates x ~18 instances has effective n far below 144 due to within-template correlation. Compute ICC from the existing 828-run campaign, then grow independent templates (~40-60) rather than instances-per-template, and report template-clustered bootstrap CIs in every table.

Keep non-compensatory headline scoring but add SWE-bench's Appendix C.5-style outcome taxonomy: logging per-stage outcomes (correct / attractive-wrong-path / other-wrong / refused) is what reveals whether failures concentrate in one stage of one template — the early-warning signal for leakage and the diagnostic SWE-bench used to show ~84% of applied patches passed zero fail-to-pass tests.

Make prompt information budget part of the benchmark spec: SWE-bench scores triple from BM25 (1.96%) to oracle (4.8%) to oracle-collapsed (9.4% Opus) purely by narrowing context toward the answer — exactly the mechanism behind CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's 94-100% saturation from leaked recipes/answer menus. Freeze 2-3 disclosure tiers (raw data only; +domain framing; +method menu), report per tier, and claim the single-digit target only at the lowest tier.

Restore difficulty via distractor-rich inputs, not trickier questions: SWE-bench difficulty is localization — performance falls with input length even as retrieval recall rises. Have the generator embed each stage's evidence inside a much larger realistic data package (decoy channels, plausible-but-irrelevant covariates whose analysis IS the attractive wrong path); difficulty then scales with package size without adding label error.

Run SWE-bench's solvability filters plus the audit it skipped: they excluded tests referencing gold-patch-invented names as 'impossible even for human developers' but never ran a human check, and the community later found many instances underspecified (SWE-bench Verified). For every CRUCIBLE-CHAIN instance, machine-verify clean-control solvability from the prompt alone, detectability of planted defects, and provable-refusal-correctness for flawed premises; blind-spot-check ~5% with humans before release.

Pre-register a canonical paired subset: GPT-4's budget-forced 25% subset made SWE-bench's cross-model tables non-parallel and cost an appendix defending representativeness; their fix was the frozen 300-item Lite. Freeze a CRUCIBLE-CHAIN Lite that every model runs in full with fixed repeats, and use paired item-level tests (McNemar/permutation) to reach significance at smaller n.

Translate the temporal-split contamination defense: version the generator, hold back >=2 never-published templates per release, and report the public-vs-holdout score gap as a standing contamination statistic — a significant positive gap is direct evidence of the recipe leakage that caused saturation, and rotation gives SWE-bench-style continual updatability.

Watch harness leniency drifting the construct: SWE-bench's auto-repair rescued 20-69% of applied patches depending on model, mixing 'can reason' with 'can format a diff' at model-dependent rates. Freeze and publish CRUCIBLE-CHAIN's answer-parsing/normalization layer, report parse-failure and repair rates per model, and score refusal via explicit schema so the flawed-premise condition isn't a parser lottery.
